sources.title: Dagobert Renouf: Selling Comp AI to $30K/month, and why he left indie making for B2B
sources.originalTitle: Dagobert Renouf on Comp AI, $30K/month in SaaS sales, and building again
sources.outlet: Morning Maker Show with Sandra and Dan
sources.summary: Dagobert recounts sponsoring his wedding suit, then closing about $200K of annual recurring revenue a month in sales at Comp AI. He explains why honest selling works, why he now picks growing markets over artistic ideas, and why he thinks the indie-making culture is a poor way to build a business.

principles.text: Sell by being real: tell poor-fit prospects it isn't for you, and the ones who need it will trust you.
principles.quote: when you push someone away who actually needs it immediately, they trust you because they know you're not selling it to them.

principles.text: Start from a growing market, not from what would be a cool idea. Building as an artist held him back.
principles.quote: I was coming to it from the perspective of an artist and not an entrepreneur.

principles.text: Find an underserved market via search demand and competitor reviews, then build an alternative with a clear differentiator.
principles.quote: finding an undeserved market where people are searching for something going to G2 or Capira looking of like existing products what's working failing building an alternative with a unique differentiator

principles.text: Look outside social-media-friendly niches. Old industries lack competition and can pay far more than cheap SaaS.
principles.quote: that you can sell a SAS for like 100 times more than $9 a month, you know

principles.text: Solo building is fragile; co-founders let you rest and split the work, with one building and one selling.
principles.quote: when you're going at it alone, you cannot have a bad day, you know. You cannot rest basically.

principles.text: Aim for a higher income bar. Founder hours at about $5K/month aren't worth it once you've seen better.
principles.quote: I was going through the craziest like 70 hours a week with zero safety for making 5k a month. It's like way too low.

sources.title: Dagobert Renouf: Burnout, authentic posting, and building Launch Day as a community
sources.originalTitle: How a Burnout Taught Me to Build a Company My Way
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf explains how he grew on X by replying to people, then burned out and switched to being himself. He covers how Launch Day (48-hour launch events with big discounts and founder interviews) works, why community matters for solo makers, and why he stopped chasing money over vision.

principles.text: Early on, grow on social by replying to people daily and making friends; once big, switch to being yourself.
principles.quote: I used to do 250 replies a day for six months or one year

principles.text: Test demand with one tweet: if 20 people say yes with money, you have product-market fit.
principles.quote: you just make a tweet and you have 20 people say yeah take my money okay you know you have something

principles.text: Tell your story and show yourself: people who care about you then check out and buy your product.
principles.quote: what works is to show myself to tell my story then people give a [ __ ] and then they check out my product and they buy it

principles.text: Limited-time launch windows and deep, negotiated discounts create FOMO and drive buying.
principles.quote: if you don't limit people don't buy don't buy it. The limit helps people buy.

principles.text: Curate who you feature: pick founders who open up and give big discounts, and be honest when the audience is not a fit.
principles.quote: I don't accept people who's not going to give a big discount because they just want like to launch on 10 platforms

principles.text: Relying entirely on social media is fragile and stressful; an algorithm change can kill you.
principles.quote: when everything depends on social media then any change in algorithm can kill you that's very very uh stressful

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf learned to start from audience problems after Logology stalled
sources.originalTitle: Dagobert Renouf — The Emotional Journey of Entrepreneurship
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf recounts building Logology with his wife, years of slow traction, and how Twitter changed his marketing and mood. He explains why his audience-first Twitter course beat the product-first Logology, and how he will rebuild Logology 2 around his audience's problems.

principles.text: Start from an audience and its problems, then build the product, instead of building first and hunting for buyers.
principles.quote: we're going to start with people's problem so I have my audience I mean my audience know like those people who follow me let's say and I just need to figure out their problem

principles.text: Sharing your own founder journey draws in fellow founders and works as soft, non-salesy customer acquisition.
principles.quote: just talking about my startup and my journey is enough to make startup Founders notice and engage and then you know after some time they get curious they check out my startup and boom

principles.text: Engage with others first; their topics fuel your best ideas, and good replies get repurposed into tweets and memes.
principles.quote: Step Zero is engage with other people because that's how I get the best ideas

principles.text: Combine authenticity with deliberate strategy rather than posting whatever you feel like.
principles.quote: I try to mix authenticity with strategy that's always been like my balance

principles.text: Be generous and self-promotional in a daily rhythm: help others first, then push your own content.
principles.quote: I'm selfless in the morning and selfish in the evening basically in the morning I engage with other people's content and in the evening it's only my tweets that matter

principles.text: Choose a co-founder you could raise a child with, since a startup forces you to confront everything under pressure.
principles.quote: you should pick someone you could have a baby with

sources.title: How Dagobert launched a Twitter course to $30K in a month: landing page first, relationships, Black Friday
sources.originalTitle: Conversation with Dagobert on Making Money with a Twitter Course [Extended Version]
sources.summary: Dagobert explains how he built and launched his Twitter course after growing his audience, covering validation via the landing page, a pre-built launch list, and a Black Friday retweet-for-discount mechanic. He also shares his view on pricing, perceived value, and preparing for platform risk.

principles.text: Write the landing page before building the product to test whether the promise is engaging and solves a big problem.
principles.quote: the first thing I did is I wrote the landing page

principles.text: Build a launch list during creation: offer to DM people you help when the product is out.
principles.quote: I would send them a reply saying hey you want me to send a DM when my course is out and so I had a list of 150 people like that

principles.text: Give generously for a long time; when you finally ask for launch support, people say yes.
principles.quote: I gave without thinking for so long that when I asked for once for some support they gave it and that was amazing

principles.text: Use a discount that requires a retweet so a link-bearing promo still gets reach and engagement.
principles.quote: I did basically 40 but if you retweet I give you 20 more so it's like 60 off if you retweet

principles.text: Perceived value tracks how close a product is to making the buyer money, which explains why courses outsell logos.
principles.quote: the closer you are to the money the higher the value

principles.text: Expect any platform or channel to end; keep savings, keep learning, and rely on portable skills like building an audience.
principles.quote: everything will end eventually so just prepare by having savings preparing that and always doing new stuff

sources.title: How Dagobert grew Logology from 200 to 4,000 Twitter followers while bootstrapping
sources.originalTitle: Interviewing Dagobert about bootstrapping Logology (episode 146)
sources.summary: Dagobert, co-founder of Logology (automated designer-quality logos for startups), talks about bootstrapping on savings after 18 months of building and ~5 sales a month. He explains how a spammy tweet led him to Twitter and the daily interaction routine that grew his audience, plus lessons on branding, pricing tiers and signup friction.

principles.text: On Twitter, spend about 10x more time interacting with others than on your own tweets.
principles.quote: you need to spend 10 times more 10 times more time on interacting with others than your own tweets

principles.text: Replies and likes put you in people's feeds for days, so consistent genuine interaction compounds your reach.
principles.quote: as soon as someone interacts with you so like they reply back or they like one of your reply to their content as soon as they do this you know that within 24 48 72 hours you're gonna show up in their feed

principles.text: Twitter beats small communities like Reddit or Indie Hackers for traffic because of its viral component.
principles.quote: it has way more power than like a community like in the hikers or like credit like there's a viral component to it that's huge

principles.text: Sharing your real emotions and frustrations publicly can hook an audience and open doors.
principles.quote: well if i share my emotions and if i share what i feel on twitter it can hook people

principles.text: You don't need a great brand to succeed, but look decent; a brand you love gives confidence and a starting edge.
principles.quote: you need to look at least decent and the second thing is usually when you get a brand that you really love for yourself it gives you a ton of confidence and it gives you a good starting point

principles.text: Removing the signup wall before showing value was what finally produced real sales.
principles.quote: just removing the need to sign up it finally got us some actual sales

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf sold $8K of a Twitter course in 24 hours with pain-first positioning
sources.originalTitle: The Secrets Behind Dagobert's Renouf Twitter Course ($8,073.30 in just 24 hours!)
sources.summary: Dagobert explains how he grew a startup audience on Twitter by sharing his journey instead of promoting his product, then used the same emotional playbook to launch a crowded-niche course. He covers aggressive positioning, a pain-to-relief sales page, building the product after the landing page, and researching pains instead of ideas.

principles.text: Share your journey instead of pitching your product; it's relatable to your target audience and drives far more engagement.
principles.quote: to grow on Twitter that it was better to not promote myself and to instead by talking about my journey

principles.text: Emotion is what produces engagement and action, so optimize content for emotional connection over direct promotion.
principles.quote: most important thing is the emotion that's how you get engagement that's how you get action

principles.text: Humor builds instant trust, creating personal-feeling connections at scale that make later conversion easier.
principles.quote: by making someone laugh you just instantly make them trust you

principles.text: In a saturated market, take a risky, polarizing stance so people notice and click through, then let the landing page convince them.
principles.quote: I'd rather call it dominate so even people who think they hate it will check the landing page and then the landing page will convince them

principles.text: Structure the sales page as pain, then absolution (it's not your fault), then the solution.
principles.quote: focus on the pain and then oh but it's not your fault here's the solution

principles.text: Write the landing page story first, then build the product to deliver that promise; it boosts reviews and word of mouth.
principles.quote: it's not like I had my course and then I tried to tell a story about it it's like I had this perfect story and then based on the perfect story I was like okay these are the chapters

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf bootstrapped Logology with a designer-in-the-loop quiz and Twitter memes
sources.originalTitle: Dagobert Renouf | Ep010 | Superflow Podcast
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf explains how he and his designer wife automated a $3,000 branding service into a roughly $100 logo product, and how Twitter (spam plugs, then personal story and memes) turned about one sale a week into six or seven. He also covers listening only to paying customers, staying focused on marketing over features, and building instead of reading.

principles.text: Productize a high-priced expert service by automating it and making it affordable.
principles.quote: we want to make what she does for three thousand dollars we want to automate it and make it affordable

principles.text: Remove bad outcomes by limiting and pre-vetting every choice the customer can make.
principles.quote: you can't go out of logology with a shitty looking logo it's not possible because we like limit every choice and vet every choice from her ahead of time

principles.text: Listen only to paying customers; non-buyers don't see the value and will pull your product off course.
principles.quote: we should only listen to people who pay us like people who actually spent money on the product

principles.text: When you don't know marketing, plug your product everywhere, then double down on the channel that works.
principles.quote: anytime there's the opportunity to plug in logology i'm gonna do it

principles.text: Personal-brand content on Twitter (story, memes) became the main sales driver.
principles.quote: growing on twitter was like the best thing i did because now i went from basically one sale per week to now about six or seven

principles.text: Resist building more features until marketing carries survival; keep saying no.
principles.quote: the whole thing for me is to say no i'm going to keep focusing on marketing

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf grew Logology and 60k Twitter followers by connecting, not just posting
sources.originalTitle: The Future of Business: Exploring EMERGING Trends and Technologies | Dagobert Renouf | VezaTalks 012
sources.summary: Dagobert explains how a startup that failed on "build it and they will come" found its only working channel in Twitter. He covers the reply-first growth method, why authenticity beats AI-copied tweets, using memes to build trust, and why founders should market as a person rather than as a company.

principles.text: Building a good product is not enough; without eyes on it, nobody cares. Marketing has to be done from day one.
principles.quote: we realized if we're not putting eyes on this product nobody's gonna care like it's not enough

principles.text: When all else fails, go all in on one channel that shows traction. Twitter scaled linearly with followers for Logology.
principles.quote: we failed at everything else we tried marketing wise we don't really have any other options so let me just go all in on Twitter and see where it takes us

principles.text: With a tiny audience, spend your time connecting (replying to others) rather than tweeting into the void. Replies carry the same viral potential as tweets.
principles.quote: instead of spending your time tweeting you need to spend your time connecting

principles.text: Reply to accounts at your own level in your niche, about 30 minutes a day. That is usually enough to reach 500 to 1000 followers.
principles.quote: spend 30 minutes a day at the beginning just looking for people who inspire you in your Niche and connecting with them replying to their stuff

principles.text: Don't copy viral tweets or lean on AI-generated ones. Audience built on borrowed content doesn't care about you, so it won't buy from you. Care from followers matters more than follower count.
principles.quote: between two times more and ten times more it doesn't change much what matters is how many people care

principles.text: Market as a person, not a company. People follow founders, which builds trust, authority and opens PR, partnership and SEO opportunities.
principles.quote: you have to use it as a person and kind of build that personal brand of your thoughts your vision

sources.title: How Logology automated $2,000 logo design into a $100 product and landed its first customer
sources.originalTitle: Get a Designer-Quality Logo for Your Startup - Dagobert Renouf Founder of Logology
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf explains how he and his designer wife turned a $2,000 custom logo service into a $100 automated questionnaire-to-logo product. He covers getting the first customer, when startups should invest in branding, and standing out in a crowded no-code market.

principles.text: Productize an expensive service by automating the expert's process so a price-constrained segment can afford it.
principles.quote: can we make the thing that we that you sell for 2 000 for like a week of work you know consulting can we make that cheap i mean not not cheap affordable you know at like 100 or 200 bucks

principles.text: Automate by copying how the expert actually works: ask discovery questions, then match to ideas.
principles.quote: we try to really copy how she works so usually the way she works is she's gonna ask questions uh from the client like what's your vision what are your values you know who's your target customer

principles.text: Build a deep, domain-specific catalog rather than generic assets, so output carries real meaning for each segment.
principles.quote: what we did in the past two and a half years is try to design a catalog of logos for every type of startup

principles.text: A product can be perfect for a few people who buy instantly; the hard part is extending that to everyone.
principles.quote: it can be very very good for a few people and then they just fall in love with it instantly and just buy it so now what's difficult is doing that with everyone

principles.text: Don't spend on a logo with zero customers; invest in branding once about 10-20 people love what you do.
principles.quote: if you have zero customers probably not time but like if you start to get a bit of traction like you found you know at least 10 or 20 people who really love what you do

principles.text: In crowded no-code markets, distinctive branding makes people pause instead of skipping, though copy and product still matter.
principles.quote: it just gives people uh a bit of like of a pause when they come to the website and instead of just skipping they're gonna check it out

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf grew his startup with Twitter story tweets, not ads
sources.originalTitle: How to grow your business using Twitter with Dagobert Renouf | Craftsman Creative Workshop 004
sources.summary: Dagobert explains how a failed paid-ads attempt pushed him to organic Twitter. He covers why Twitter has no reach ceiling, why personal story tweets beat memes and guru one-liners, and why a face-and-name account beats a brand account. He also covers engaging first to get shown and how a small audience can still pay off.

principles.text: Pick Twitter over Indie Hackers because its reach has no ceiling; focus there and it keeps compounding.
principles.quote: Twitter the ceiling is kind of infinite so that's what convinced me to focus on Twitter instead

principles.text: Turn events into a problem-and-solution story with a lesson, not a flat status update.
principles.quote: if you can transform that into today I had this problem then I found this solution and now this gives me hope for XYZ then it's like 10 times more powerful

principles.text: Drop the guru one-liners; share your own experience for more humility, authenticity and traction.
principles.quote: instead of trying to make a big sentence that teaches people everything I was like let's just start with I like I experiened this today like this happened to me way simpler way more humility and way more authentic

principles.text: Personal story tweets convert viewers to followers better than memes, which get laughs but no curiosity.
principles.quote: when you write a story that's more personal then they're curious and that's I think the core of my you know quote unquote success on Twitter it's actually the story tweets

principles.text: Build the account on your real face and name; people bond with people more than with brands.
principles.quote: there's nothing better than using your face your name um and being the most uh authentic you can be about who you are

principles.text: To get early likes, engage with people you resonate with first; Twitter then shows your tweets to them.
principles.quote: you have to engage first like you basically have to start engage with other people

sources.title: Dagobert Renouf on Twitter growth: small goals, personal brands, and not quitting channels too early
sources.originalTitle: New Twitter Growth Strategies 2022 (Dagobert Renouf Interview)
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf (Logology founder) explains why big ambition causes perfectionism and how focusing on small goals gets him shipping. He covers why personal brands beat company accounts, why repeating content kills Twitter engagement, and why channels like affiliates need time before you judge them.

principles.text: Keep big dreams but focus on small goals; they keep you executing instead of paralyzed.
principles.quote: have small goals like keep having Big Dreams to like focus on like small goals

principles.text: An outsized ambition fuels perfectionism, because you try to guarantee an outcome you can't guarantee.
principles.quote: if I was stuck in this ambition I would be stuck in perfectionism to try to reassure myself that it's gonna be achieved

principles.text: Avoid both extremes: don't polish forever, and don't launch a weekend project and quit. Give a validated idea a real go.
principles.quote: maybe it's good to spend one month or two months on something if you have some pre-validation some hints it can work

principles.text: Don't give up on an acquisition channel too soon; it can take months to pay off, but change what isn't working.
principles.quote: if you give up too soon like I could have stopped the affiliation after three months and say oh I don't want to keep you know losing 30 a month but now it's making us like 400 a month

principles.text: If you build products around one topic, build a personal brand rather than a company account; it's far easier to grow.
principles.quote: basically it's 10 times easier to build an audience for a person than for a brand that's obvious because it's like people relate

principles.text: Repeating the same content wears out your audience; keep your content fresh and evolve it after the first year.
principles.quote: if I make the same joke a hundred times eventually it's less funny and it's it's normal you know like people get bored

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf grew from 150 to 15k Twitter followers and bootstrapped Logology
sources.originalTitle: Live Interview with Dagobert Renouf
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf explains how he turned Twitter into Logology's main marketing channel by connecting one-on-one and sharing his founder story. He also covers bootstrapping for freedom, automating his wife's design process into a product, and waiting to launch on Product Hunt until there is momentum.

principles.text: On Twitter, connect one-on-one with people instead of broadcasting like a TED talk.
principles.quote: if you're just like a normal guy or like a startup founder it's all about connecting one-on-one with people so going to people's profile looking at what they do

principles.text: Share your own startup story daily; founders who relate to it are your target customers and become buyers.
principles.quote: basically it's all about sharing my experience and what what happens is other startup founders relate to it and because good news is startup founders well they're my target customers

principles.text: Only plug your product when it is relevant and adds value to the conversation; otherwise it is spam.
principles.quote: the difference is is it relevant is it done with like kind of uh humility like and do you are you trying to be nice and to bring value and or are you just trying to plug your product

principles.text: Skip big VC-oriented startup books when you are tiny and unfunded; experiment yourself and focus on marketing.
principles.quote: i would advise people to not read too much into the big startup books because it doesn't necessarily apply to you if you're tiny and it's a trap because it can make you overthink everything

principles.text: Launch on Product Hunt only once you have a solid product, happy customers and an audience to create momentum.
principles.quote: you wait until you have a pretty solid product happy customers you build some kind of audience around it and that way when you launch you have all that momentum with you

principles.text: Productize an expert's craft by pre-building vetted options and automating the matching, delivering expert quality cheaply.
principles.quote: it's really like we made her into kind of like an automated system okay behind the scenes it's her who worked tirelessly to create all the possibilities

sources.title: How Logology's Dagobert Renouf turned marketing into participating and service work into a product
sources.originalTitle: Startup Story 02 "Logology": A 🇫🇷 startup disrupting the creative design market
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf, co-founder of Logology, explains how he went from spamming "what are you building" threads to participating on Twitter, why organic beat paid for his bootstrapped startup, and how he automated a designer's service workflow into a product. He also covers staying motivated through hopeless stretches.

principles.text: Add a negative motivation: what you refuse to go back to keeps you building when no customers show up.
principles.quote: to have like a negative motivation so what i mean by that is like not just something i want to reach so like help the world with like amazing brands when they're just starting but also what i want to avoid

principles.text: Replace "marketing" with "participating": join communities, meet and engage people instead of promoting yourself.
principles.quote: so what really helped me was that was like switching from marketing to participating and it's also way more fun

principles.text: Real marketing is connecting and listening, promoting your product only when it's useful.
principles.quote: real marketing is about connecting with people listening to people uh and trying to obviously promote your product when it's useful you know but that's it

principles.text: When you're new and unknown, organic beats paid because people trust it; Dagobert's paid tests (Google ads, newsletters) gave no sales.
principles.quote: when you're new and nobody knows you organic is so cool because people trust it way more

principles.text: Build the product by automating what you already do for clients as a service, balancing personalization with automation.
principles.quote: we basically took like everything she does with clients like that she just described and like try to make it into an automated way

principles.text: Pick work you enjoy, because enjoyment is what keeps you going when a good idea starts to look bad.
principles.quote: if you don't enjoy it you're going to give up when it's like this exact time that you should actually okay i'm not sure but i enjoy it so i keep doing anyway

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf grew Logology by sharing his real founder story on Twitter
sources.originalTitle: How a Startup switched their focus to Marketing and exponentially grew
sources.summary: After 13 months averaging one user a week and failed paid channels, Dagobert went all-in on Twitter, sharing his struggles and memes. The community that formed recommended his product (even non-customers) and brought backlinks, partnerships and interviews. He also covers topic keywords, repurposing replies into tweets, and batch scheduling.

principles.text: Share your real struggles, not networking pitches; authentic vulnerability builds a community that recommends you.
principles.quote: the more vulnerable and authentic i am on twitter the stronger this community gets

principles.text: People who like you as a founder will recommend your product even if they never bought it.
principles.quote: nine out of 10 people who recommend it they never bought anything they just like me and what i'm doing

principles.text: Paid marketing doesn't substitute for hustle; you can't just pay money and get money without a lot of testing budget.
principles.quote: you can't just like pay money and then you make money like it's like i mean to get to that point you will need so much money to make testing

principles.text: Use the exact topic keywords in every tweet to get reach beyond your followers; the algorithm doesn't understand synonyms.
principles.quote: if you want to be trending in the marketing topic you need to use the word marketing

principles.text: Repurpose replies that did well into standalone posts; they act as an MVP proving the idea works.
principles.quote: it's kind of like you know an mvp for my tweets like oh people liked it so then i can repurpose as a stand-alone tweet

principles.text: One social channel done well compounds into backlinks, partnerships, interviews and credibility without extra effort.
principles.quote: i get about one new backlink every day doing nothing specific about it just from twitter

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf took Logology from a failed launch to $3k/month by going all-in on Twitter
sources.originalTitle: Why your product needs marketing - Dagobert Renouf, Logology
sources.summary: Dagobert shares how Logology, a logo and brand design service he runs with his wife, flopped at launch after building for nearly two years. He then found traction by spamming his link, going all-in on Twitter, and sharing his journey publicly, reaching roughly $2-3k/month. He also reflects on chasing money versus fulfillment.

principles.text: Launching to a waiting list is not marketing; you need a real, repeatable distribution plan.
principles.quote: we like talked about it on the reddit and in the hackers so we were watching everyone and not understanding why everybody wasn't buying

principles.text: Don't build more features to fix a distribution problem; the missing piece is marketing.
principles.quote: we ended up having no way of doing marketing and then we did what every person does when they have no way of doing marketing is build more features to fix it

principles.text: A product doesn't speak for itself; you must market it even if you dislike it.
principles.quote: i'm the guy who wants the product to speak for itself look at my work and [ __ ] buy it and you know and i don't want anything else

principles.text: When you have no channel, try everything and show up in every relevant conversation until one channel responds.
principles.quote: i'm just gonna spam i'm just gonna put my link everywhere like an idiot every occasion i get i'm gonna say oh you need to check out the gology

principles.text: Share your real journey publicly; transparent building-in-public content can go viral and drive sales.
principles.quote: it showed me that sharing what i was going through with twitter oh and i got a sales probably out of pity

principles.text: Relying on a single channel is exhausting; diversify into SEO and earned media (podcasts, articles) that compound.
principles.quote: having sales come from twitter only it's exhausting because like if you don't tweet for one day well if you don't tweet for one day well nobody comes to your website

sources.title: Dago on the dark side of indie life: exits, passive income myths and overworking
sources.originalTitle: Nico and Dago talk about the dark side of entrepreneurship
sources.summary: Dago launches the new This Indie Life format with Nico, focused on the unglamorous side of bootstrapping. He shares lessons from his failed logo startup, why passive income is a myth, why indies should plan an exit, and how overwork and success highs derail founders.

principles.text: Social media's success-only feed makes founders feel like failures, so share the hard parts honestly.
principles.quote: when you open social media and only see success at least for me I start to feel like a failure real fast

principles.text: Don't over-invest in quality for a market that won't pay for it; match effort to what buyers actually value.
principles.quote: mistake we did is we went after a market that is like doesn't have much money and like we went at it with like highest quality like every logo is designed by hand

principles.text: Passive income is a myth: earning without working demands huge active effort first.
principles.quote: it's so active like it's the opposite it's active income like it takes so much work to make money without working

principles.text: Avoid emotional attachment to your company and plan an exit if you want to stay indie.
principles.quote: I think now at least if you want to stay Indie you need to plan an exit

principles.text: If sustaining the business requires extreme hours for years, the product itself may be wrong.
principles.quote: if you need to work this hard for this long maybe it's the wrong product you know

principles.text: Success highs breed overconfidence; keep doing the things that brought you the win.
principles.quote: when you get the high you can make mistakes because now because you're high on like the success

sources.title: Why Dago shut down Logology after 5 years: business fundamentals, burnout and going back to a job
sources.originalTitle: Dago quits his startup
sources.summary: Dago explains why he and his wife closed their bootstrapped logo startup Logology after five years: no recurring revenue, constant customer-acquisition pressure, AI uncertainty and a health-wrecking burnout. His main lesson is to start from business fundamentals (demand, willingness to pay, acquisition cost) rather than a cool idea and hard work.

principles.text: Hard work and a good idea don't make a business; only the fundamentals of a good business do.
principles.quote: we were idealistic and thought having a good idea and working hard was enough to succeed

principles.text: Start from the boring business fundamentals: demand, willingness to pay, and customer acquisition cost.
principles.quote: is there demand are customers paying for it enough can you acquire customers at a good enough cost like all the boring

principles.text: Without recurring revenue you must re-win customers every month, which creates relentless pressure.

sources.summary: Dago relaunches This Indie Life solo after burning out, divorcing and leaving a job. He picks content (podcast, book, course, newsletter) as the fastest route to 4K a month, explains why going solo lowered his required revenue, and why he now shares the hard parts and takes sponsors.

principles.text: When you need runway, pick the fastest path to revenue with assets you already have, and make survival the focus.
principles.quote: so my focus is survival and make money and the quickest pass for me is content podcast my book and my courses

principles.text: Lower the income you need to cover your life; a smaller target removes pressure and makes solo work viable.
principles.quote: now that I'm alone to make a basic living it's I don't even need to make 5K a month I have to make 4K a month

principles.text: Avoid being pulled between opposing modes of work; context switching between social and product building drove his burnout.
principles.quote: I was struggling with context switching always switching context was impossible for me

principles.text: Share the dark side of the founder journey, not just wins; honesty builds community and resonates more than success stories.
principles.quote: I want to share my journey you know how much I love sharing my journey even the dirty and like very dark side of it that's really what I love

principles.text: Don't be precious about monetizing; take sponsors, but only products you genuinely love and be transparent about it.
principles.quote: I burnt out and I realized it was the stupidest thing to not take money or anything like this is a business guys

principles.text: Choose work that is easy and natural for you rather than restarting the startup grind of finding product-market fit.
principles.quote: it's only one thing it's only writing thinking and connecting with people so like to me that's way easier

sources.title: Burnout, therapy and founder ego: Dago's lessons on perfectionism and picking the right platform
sources.originalTitle: 29: Lukas and Dago talk about burnout and therapy
sources.summary: Dago hosts a candid talk with Lukas (Stage Timer) about burnout, therapy and comparison on Twitter. His own takeaways: perfectionism and pride sank his last startup, therapy exposes ego-driven product mistakes, and social growth depends on where your audience actually is. Mostly mindset, with a few distribution points.

principles.text: Perfectionism kills startups: ship clean-enough work in days instead of polishing for months.
principles.quote: that's one of the big reasons I failed my previous startup is I was always trying to do everything perfectly and spending months on things that could have taken weeks or even days sometimes

principles.text: Wasted build time is often ego and fear of failure, not a product need. Someone outside your bubble can expose it.
principles.quote: it's not because of the useless features it's about I had my pride of I want this product to be perfect because I was scared of failing

principles.text: Treat therapy between co-founders like routine maintenance, at least monthly.
principles.quote: if tomorrow I start a new startup and I have a co-founder I will do couples therapy with them

principles.text: On social media, audience presence matters more than content type. Post where your buyers actually hang out.
principles.quote: it doesn't so much matter the platform in terms of like content but it what matters is like who uses it

principles.text: Stop building for other indie hackers; their problems are solved. Find other industries with unsolved problems.
principles.quote: stop building for other developers all their problems have been solved

principles.text: Don't say yes to money that your heart isn't in; it leads to burnout and the wrong life.
principles.quote: if it's not what your heart wants you end up not in the right life and then you burn out and you're unhappy

sources.title: Dago on Twitter growth: batching content, link handling, credibility at 10K, and avoiding burnout
sources.originalTitle: Dago has burnout, James sells bifold wallets
sources.summary: Dago explains why he burned out after launching his course, how he batches two months of tweets in one week, and why links kill tweet reach unless you make people curious or incentivize engagement. He also shares how 10K followers changed perceived credibility, and why living and building real stories beats rehashing strategy.

principles.text: Too many open threads cause lost direction, lost productivity and burnout; clear the backlog to recover.
principles.quote: basically when I get too many things I get lost and I lose direction and when I lose direction I lose productivity and I burn out quickly

principles.text: Batch your content: go all-in for one week and write two months of tweets ahead of time.
principles.quote: I hide two months of content ahead of time let's basically just go all in for one week and write a ton of stuff

principles.text: Crossing a follower threshold like 10K boosts perceived credibility and directly lifts product sales.
principles.quote: reaching 10K for example was the biggest change in how people perceive me like it was crazy like it's just like the number of sales of my product just like improved overnight because people thought I was more credible

principles.text: Spend time building and experiencing things so you have fresh, raw stories to tweet about, instead of rehashing strategy.
principles.quote: it's better if I spend my time building or like experiencing [ __ ] and then tweeting about it then if I just like I did for the past year to spend all of my time tweeting

principles.text: Links hurt reach because people leave instead of engaging; make the tweet curious enough to engage without the link, or incentivize engagement.

principles.text: Short subtitled clips (around 15 seconds) can drive podcast listeners from Twitter.
principles.quote: if you can get like a 15 seconds bite of the show with like subtitles and a cool bit that will probably do well

principles.text: Build what comes from inside and helps people; that is what makes work meaningful.
principles.quote: really what makes it meaningful is that it comes from like inside like it's like really something that I want to give

principles.text: Know your real driver. Copying other indie hackers' lifestyle goals led to burnout; his driver is contributing and supporting others.
principles.quote: my driver is different my driver is more like arid and my driver is more like I want to contribute I want to help I want to support others

principles.text: Lower your expectations of a job and you perform better at it.
principles.quote: I actually feel way better at this job now I'm like you know I'm way more productive because I don't expect too much from it

principles.quote: it's obvious that the course hasn't been updated in a year so it's kind of like scary to people

sources.title: Back to indie hacking after burning $100k: build financial freedom before the next startup bet
sources.originalTitle: Back to indie hacking after burning $100k
sources.summary: After losing $100k and his marriage to a failed startup, Dagobert Renouf resets his approach. He rebuilds health and runway, then monetizes existing assets (audience, podcast, course, consulting) to reach about $6k/month before risking another startup.

principles.text: Startups are bets you rarely win, and success is never fully in your control, even with validation and product-market fit.
principles.quote: Building a startup is like placing a bet. I can win (rarely) or I can lose (often). And the game never stops until I sell the company or quit.

principles.text: Platform dependency is a core risk: algorithm, pricing or policy changes, or a big player's feature launch, can wipe out a business overnight.
principles.quote: changes in social or SEO algorithms can reduce traffic by 90% and kill growth

principles.text: Secure financial freedom first via the most efficient revenue that doesn't sell your time, instead of betting everything on one crazy idea.
principles.quote: I won’t put all my hopes of financial freedom into a crazy startup idea again. Instead, I’m going for the most efficient way to get revenue without selling my time.

principles.text: Monetize assets you've already built (audience, podcast, course) before chasing something new; obsessive focus on one startup blinds you to obvious revenue.
principles.quote: Since I wasn’t focused on financial freedom, only obsessed about growing my startup, I missed on obvious revenue generating opportunities.

principles.text: Stack several small bets (ebook, sponsors, course refresh, high-priced consulting) to reach a sustainable income floor.
principles.quote: With these 4 small bets, I think I can reach $6k per month, mostly on auto-pilot.

principles.text: Build a runway and income floor first so you can afford to take startup risk again from a stable position.
principles.quote: Once I get there, I’ll be in a better position to take the risk of building startups again.

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf bootstrapped Logology and grew a Twitter audience from 150 to 40k
sources.originalTitle: Dagobert Renouf, Co-Founder of Logology (IdeaMensch interview)
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf shares how he and his wife built Logology, an automated logo and brand identity tool, after two years building and two years struggling with marketing. Twitter, used to share his founder journey, became the channel that finally worked. He also covers timeboxing, slow growth and building in public.

principles.text: Build in public: sharing your founder journey on Twitter drives traffic, partnerships and customers when paid ads failed.
principles.quote: Then in the summer of 2021, I started tweeting about my journey. Eventually, I noticed more people were coming to my website, talking about my product, and recommending us to other founders.

principles.text: Make audience-building a daily habit; about 2h/day on Twitter produced 10x traffic, podcast invites and partners.
principles.quote: So I made it a part of my daily routine and now spend about 2h a day on it. Which led us to get 10x more traffic per day, being invited on 10+ podcasts, finding new partners, and so on.

principles.text: Be the public face of your company; sharing openly opens doors to customers, partners and investors.
principles.quote: You are the public face of your company and have a lot to win by connecting with the world directly.

principles.text: Start from a first-hand problem: automate an expensive service to cut price while keeping quality.
principles.quote: we looked for a way to make it cheaper without losing the quality. Eventually, we stumbled upon the idea of automating the brand research and design aspects and cut the price by 10.

principles.text: Persist through marketing failure by trying different ideas until one channel works.
principles.quote: But I didn’t want to quit and decided to keep trying different marketing ideas. And one day I found the right one (growing a Twitter audience).

principles.text: You don't need to grow fast; a slow small business that never quits can still grow every year.
principles.quote: You don’t need to go fast to succeed. All you need is to never quit.

sources.title: How Dagobert Renouf sold logo spots on his wedding suit and landed a sales job
sources.originalTitle: I put company logos on my suit to pay for my wedding. It led to a new job. (Business Insider, as told to)
sources.summary: Dagobert Renouf, a bootstrapped founder short on cash, asked his audience for help paying for his wedding and turned their joke into a stunt: selling logo spots on his suit to fellow entrepreneurs for about 10,000 euros. The stunt shows how to use a community, persistence and quality execution, and it led to an unexpected sales job.

principles.text: Build in public and ask your audience openly; the best idea can come back from the community.
principles.quote: I posted something like, "I have to find a way to pay for my wedding. No idea how I'm going to do it."

principles.text: Get out of your comfort zone and try crazy ideas if you want to make it as an entrepreneur.
principles.quote: You've got to get out of your comfort zone. You try crazy shit if you want to make it.

principles.text: Connect an unusual idea to what the people involved care about to bring them on board.
principles.quote: What made her come around, and what was making this whole thing beautiful, was when I really connected it to the fact that it was a way to bring my community to our wedding.

principles.text: Great ideas look crazy first and obvious later, so keep pushing through months of public skepticism.
principles.quote: At first, they think you're crazy, and then it seems obvious.

principles.text: Execution quality matters: make a sponsored stunt look premium so it reads as credible, not as a joke.
principles.quote: Once I started doing the suit, then I'm like, "OK, now I want it to look good. I don't want to look like an idiot."

principles.text: Visibility around a bold public idea attracts unexpected opportunities, like a job offer from someone who kept engaging.
principles.quote: Without the suit, I would have never gotten this job.

sources.title: Why 100K followers didn't save my startup: build a real product and non-social distribution
sources.originalTitle: Having 100K followers won't make your product successful
sources.summary: Dagobert recounts building 100K X followers while his 5-year startup never exceeded $4K/month. Audience helped early (to $3K MRR) but hit diminishing returns at 10K followers, and chasing followers made him neglect fixing the product and building other channels. Success requires a real problem, a great product, and at least one durable distribution channel.

principles.text: A big following is a consequence of success, not its cause; don't assume successful founders got there via followers.
principles.quote: The fact that they have followers is a consequence of sharing their journey towards success, not the reason for their success in the first place.

principles.text: Business success requires three things: a real problem solved, a great product, and at least one distribution channel.
principles.quote: To make it big in business, you need to solve a real problem + build a great product + figure out at least one distribution channel. There is no way around it.

principles.text: Social audience gives strong early gains but diminishing returns past a few thousand to 10K followers.
principles.quote: Building my audience did help us grow from $300 to $3,000 monthly revenue at the beginning.

principles.text: When a channel plateaus and eats your time, step back, fix the product and build other channels instead of chasing vanity followers.
principles.quote: At this point I should’ve taken a step back, focus on fixing my product, and built other distribution channels.

principles.text: Successful founders with big audiences pair solving real problems with long-term acquisition channels like affiliation or SEO.
principles.quote: they build long-term acquisition channels like affiliation or SEO

principles.text: Grow to a few thousand followers early for friends, partnerships, media and initial traffic, then get back into the trenches of building the business.
principles.quote: But once you start to be a little bit established, your time is better spent being in the trenches and doing the hard work of growing a real business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert recounts sponsoring his wedding suit, then closing about $200K of annual recurring revenue a month in sales at Comp AI. He explains why honest selling works, why he now picks growing markets over artistic ideas, and why he thinks the indie-making culture is a poor way to build a business.

chunks.heading: Why Dagobert argues indie making is a lottery, and what he sees as the "scam"
chunks.text:
- Dagobert posted that indie making is a lottery and says he took heavy criticism for it. He compares it to telling a believer that "Jesus isn't real".
- He stands by it mostly. His point: Comp AI "got incredibly lucky to stumble upon this at the right time". Timing and market matter more than anything.
- The "scam" he describes is not entrepreneurship itself. It is the indie-making culture of "hey, I made millions by doing this, here's my MRR every month", where people mostly sell to other indie makers.
- It works like a pyramid: a few people at the top (he names Pieter Levels and Marc Lou) benefit as others buy their books, courses and boilerplates. He says these people do cool work and monetizing followers is fine.
- Survivorship bias: social media shows only the winners, so "it seems normal and easy". He calls selling to the indie-maker community "one of the hardest ways to be an entrepreneur" if you want to get rich.
- Criticizing a big name brings their fans after you, which he sees as unhealthy, almost cult-like.

chunks.heading: How he says to pick a market instead
chunks.text:
- His main mistake over seven years of failing: he came "from the perspective of an artist and not an entrepreneur", building things that would be "cool" (a designer-quality $90 logo, a Product Hunt alternative that cares about founders), never asking "what's a growing market right now."
- Once you have the right market, "you don't have to do much". Years of indie making already gave him the skills (SEO, product), so the market is the missing piece.
- His method:
  - Do SEO research for underserved markets where people are searching.
  - Browse G2 and Capterra to see which products work or fail.
  - Build an alternative with a clear differentiator, such as different pricing.
  - Reach buyers through traditional channels: sales calls or outreach.
- He calls this "way better and way easier" than social media, especially for people who aren't naturally good at social.
- He sees opportunity in "old traditional business" sectors outside social-friendly and SEO-friendly verticals. At Comp AI he sold to a freight cargo shipping boat management software company using AI to disrupt. Incumbents have no competition, so they build poorly.
- He says Comp AI won because its founder came from indie making: a Next.js product against "[bleep]" competitors.
- Those niches can sustain SaaS priced at "100 times more than $9 a month".

chunks.heading: Sponsoring his wedding suit as a distribution stunt
chunks.text:
- Context (July 2025): nearly out of money, launch day wasn't earning, and he wanted to marry his Russian partner partly because of visa limits. The smallest wedding was about €4,000, more than his remaining runway.
- Daniel Vassallo offered a $4,000 loan. A joke from the creator of Prompt Watch ("€500 if you put my logo on your suit") turned into a real offer, and he opened the suit to logo sponsors.
- Execution details:
  - He hired a stylist who makes his own coats, designed a monochrome white-logo suit, and made the suit good rather than a joke.
  - Prices ran from about €300 for small spots to about €1,500 for the large back area.
  - Hiring a videographer cost nearly €2,000, so he made little profit. He says people who paid most got the worst-placed spots, since the viral coverage focused on the cheaper ones.
- It went viral far beyond Twitter: newspapers, a relative's elderly grandfather in a Russian village, and now a Japanese TV documentary.
- Sales lesson: some people who "pledged" didn't pay until pushed. He publicly shamed one for not following through. People often assume you are joking, so you must ask for the money.
- Logo tip from his five years running a logo startup: a good logo must work in one color, and should carry the brand name unless you're Nike.
- Real purpose: to "feel the support of the community" when he needed it. About 90% of sponsors were people he knew.

chunks.heading: How he got into sales at Comp AI and what he earned
chunks.text:
- Selling suit sponsors showed him he loved sales ("you talk to someone and in five minutes they send you 500, 1,000").
- Comp AI CEO Lewis Carhart, who had sponsored his earlier launch product, saw the suit and they started talking. Dagobert offered to help sell, and joined around August 2025, before the October wedding.
- He had interviewed about 70 founders for his launch platform and says Lewis was the only one he thought could become a billionaire.
- Comp AI sells compliance (SOC 2 and similar) to startups. It reached roughly $400K ARR within months of its Product Hunt launch, partly through the founder's own selling.
- Results:
  - Sold about $200K of annual recurring revenue per month at peak, mostly from inbound demos booked as the brand went viral.
  - Earned about $30K/month pre-tax.
  - Closed about 250 deals over the year, with only about 4 churns, the lowest churn on the team. Later hires outperformed his close rate by roughly 10-15%.
- Team grew from about 5-6 people when he joined to about 30 when he left, and he lost the autonomy, the small-team feel and some of his usefulness. He was also in France while the company hired in the US.
- He says he cannot discuss the company's viral social persona and was not involved in it.

chunks.heading: His sales approach: be real and push people away
chunks.text:
- Before this he saw sales as a "job for idiots"; he was afraid his style would not work.
- His method, once in a flow state: "push people away". He tells prospects up front "I don't think it's for you, man" and documents why.
- Why it works:
  - It protects your energy at about 10 real conversations a day.
  - Telling someone who actually needs the product that it isn't for them builds immediate trust, and "you win" against competitors.
- He says you don't have to be the "used car salesman"; being genuine leaves everyone happy, which also explains the low churn.
- He argues many people avoid sales because of that stereotype, so skilled, honest sellers are scarce and valuable. He had multiple strong offers right after leaving.

chunks.heading: Lessons on money, ambition and working alone
chunks.text:
- Making 30K/month changed his view of indie making: he was "fighting for my life" for a $5K/month goal. He now says that after 70-hour weeks with no safety net, $5K/month is "way too low" and "not worth it". He wouldn't get out of bed without a shot at around $50K.
- He says succeeding for one year at Comp AI taught him far more than seven years of failure, and that glorifying going it alone is "completely stupid": solo, you cannot take a bad day or a free-minded vacation.
- He wants co-founders now: someone builds, he sells.
- Ideas he favors:
  - Take a high-paying job first. He says earning $200-300K is easier than succeeding as an entrepreneur, and raises your standard before you return to building (Daniel Vassallo earned about $400K at Amazon before indie making).
  - Ship quick fun side projects with zero revenue pressure to keep momentum, while the real bet is a B2B product that uses sales.
- Perfectionism: at his peak he took nine months to ship a one-page site (launch day), and had never launched on Product Hunt. He spent about six months vibe-coding an AI therapist partly to work through it.
- He cut his Twitter use because the feed distorts thinking: "The best way to have good tweets is to not be on Twitter." He worries about playing the spicy, controversial role for engagement.
- Side project: a tool where people sponsor his Twitter profile, which made $3,000 in about five hours of work. He notes it feels like "nothing" now versus the past.
- Current plan (September 2026 interview): about 9 months of runway with a baby due, building B2B with co-founders while shipping fun projects on Twitter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf explains how he grew on X by replying to people, then burned out and switched to being himself. He covers how Launch Day (48-hour launch events with big discounts and founder interviews) works, why community matters for solo makers, and why he stopped chasing money over vision.

chunks.heading: Burning out on social-media growth, then rebuilding around honesty and community
chunks.text:
Dagobert was a freelancer for about 12 years before founding a startup. He ran Logology (a logo generator) with his then-partner for 5 years, burned out in the process, and recovered over roughly two years. He treats that burnout as the turning point for how he builds now.

- He first burned out at around 25, when freelance clients finally arrived all at once. The survival adrenaline vanished once money came in, and he refunded about half the projects.
- He assumed his own startup would not burn him out because "motivation comes from inside". He was wrong.
- The second burnout hit right after success. Logology made about 4-5k a month and his Twitter course made about 10k a month, so about 15k a month combined, after 5 years of mostly zero and 2 years of 2-3k.
- Reaching the 10k goal solved nothing. Taxes in France ate the gains, he could not afford an apartment, and he realized he was unhappy in his relationship.
- Symptoms: a racing heart (resting normally 55-60, but 90 sitting and 130 standing), near-fainting, and being unable to get out of bed. He thought it was long COVID for 5 weeks. Naming it as burnout and depression improved his symptoms about 50% instantly.

chunks.heading: What changed after the burnout
chunks.text:
- He now focuses on purpose more than money.
- He no longer builds on a "if we hit X, everything will be fine" milestone, because the 10k milestone proved empty.
- He stopped sacrificing his vision to grow: "[ __ ] money." He accepts the risk because last time money did not fix his deeper problems.
- He spent 8 months in a salaried job at a Paris startup, Abbyal, which gave him financial security and let him recover.
- He observes that many products he loved turned bad once they sold or chased growth. He refuses to follow that path with Launch Day.
- He keeps Launch Day affordable for indie makers and will not charge more than about 100 euros, even though that limits revenue. He also keeps doing the long founder interviews.
- He is looking for side income because the model is not yet sustainable financially.

chunks.heading: Twitter/X growth: the strategy changes by stage
chunks.text:
Dagobert distinguishes how he grew from how he posts now.

- **Early (about 4 years ago):** he replied to people asking "what are you working on today?" with a link to Logology, roughly 10 times a day. One reply took off and brought 2 sales in a day, which was huge for them.
- **Growth phase:** he then did about 250 replies a day for 6 months to a year. It was effectively networking: engaging, making friends, and finding relevant content to post.
- **Results:** Logology went from about 200 a month to 3,000 a month in 6 months. He went from 0 to about 6,000 followers, and he grew from about 10K to 50K after that. His course covers this path, updated for the new algorithm.
- **Cost:** it was exhausting. Being dependent on social media is stressful because one algorithm change can kill you.
- **Now (large audience):** he posts whatever he wants, including very personal things. He lost some followers for a while, then found people liked the authenticity.
- **His view on sequencing:** he said in his course that once you are big you should stop trying to make friends and start being yourself, and he thinks starting with zero followers and full authenticity is very scary.
- **Takeaway for newcomers:** he is not sure everybody can start authentic. He would not have had the confidence to do this at zero followers.

chunks.heading: The wedding suit as a sponsorship product
chunks.text:
- Dagobert needed about 4,000 euros for a bare-minimum wedding (20 guests) while he had about 6,000 euros left and no family backup.
- He tweeted about it. Daniel Vasalo offered a 4,000 loan, the first money he had ever accepted from anyone.
- Someone then joked they would pay $500 to put their startup's logo on his suit. He retweeted asking if anyone else wanted to, and about 20 people said yes. He says: "that's product market fit."
- He took it seriously after that. He hired a stylist (a designer who had made thousands of suits) he had previously paid about 3,000 euros, and worked with him for a week on the design.
- The suit costs about 3,000 and has logo spots sold to indie makers. The best back spot is a bidding, with the top bid at 1,600 euros. One friend bought a large spot for 800 euros.
- He planned a QR-code option, a spot on the sleeve/heart area at 100 euros or less, so low-budget makers can take part, since many only had 50-100.
- He framed it to his fiancée as bringing "my people" to a wedding where he has almost no friends attending. It also makes the wedding feel interesting to him instead of boring.
- Wedding presents can be framed as business expenses, which he calls a joke.

chunks.heading: Why community matters to him
chunks.text:
- Indie makers often live in small cities with nobody to share the journey with. He has one close friend who is not on the same path.
- The community moved from indiehikers.com (5 years ago, now dead) to Twitter, which he says is less lively than 3 years ago because some people left over Elon's politics.
- "You need people to be able to share the journey with... just being alone doing that it's too hard."
- This was what helped him through the burnout and why he wants the wedding to include the community.

chunks.heading: Launch Day: a product launch event, not a Product Hunt clone
chunks.text:
- **Origin:** in September 2024 he was fed up with Product Hunt. He thinks it is still worth launching on (only upside), but says almost nobody actually visits it. He also pointed to press articles aimed at investors saying that, because Product Hunt is owned by VC, its portfolio companies get pushed, so "it's not a fair game."
- **Validation:** his first tweet pitching a better version drew huge traction. He sold about 60 spots at $29 in one week. He then waited 9 months to launch because of his burnout and divorce.
- **Why he changed the format:** copying Product Hunt would be useless. What he knows works is showing yourself and telling your story, so people care and then buy.
- **How it works:**
  - It runs once or twice a month, for 48 hours only.
  - About 15 products take part, each with a unique, limited-time discount. The limit creates fear of missing out and he says people don't buy without it.
  - He negotiates hard for the biggest discounts.
  - Each founder gets a long interview (half an hour to an hour), published as the Launch Day podcast. That averages about one interview a day.
  - Two months in, it broke even at about 3,000 a month, so he can stay at zero.
- **Selection:** he rejects founders who won't open up or who won't give a real discount, and he is honest about fit. For example, an education-for-kids product might not sell because his audience is mostly indie makers.
- **The anchor-founder tactic:** each launch includes at least one "star" with strong social media skills (e.g. Sergey, the screen-recording app maker) who carries the less experienced founders. He says: "I'm just trying to move the boat forward."
- **Community layer:** he opened a Slack with a channel per launch where founders boost and support each other, and it now has messages daily.

chunks.heading: Interviewing and content format
chunks.text:
- He does no prep and no editing, starting because he lacked time. Listeners told him they prefer it because it feels like being with the person.
- He finds hard cuts in other podcasts annoying. His approach is a free-flowing long conversation, with 30-second shorts cut separately for discovery.
- He argues "there's value in not trying to focus on value": listeners are at the gym or driving, so it need not be dense.
- He advised the host to publish unedited, since editing (the host spends about 12 hours per episode) is the reason he quit his own earlier podcast.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf recounts building Logology with his wife, years of slow traction, and how Twitter changed his marketing and mood. He explains why his audience-first Twitter course beat the product-first Logology, and how he will rebuild Logology 2 around his audience's problems.

chunks.heading: Founding with a partner: Dagobert and Lucy on logology
chunks.text:
- Dagobert and his wife Lucy built logology together. Lucy is the designer, he is the developer and business/marketing side. Roles formed organically, so they rarely need to work on the same task.
- They kept money separate for about 10 years, then merged it when they started the startup, after roughly 8 years together.
- He says the real test for a co-founder is: "pick someone you could have a baby with." If you couldn't resolve parenting disagreements with them, a startup will surface the same conflicts, because skin in the game makes it "crisis mode for a long time."
- A previous co-founder (about one year) didn't work out. That person pushed for funding and YC; when Dagobert and Lucy prepared for it, they realized it wasn't who they wanted to be.
- Commitment mismatch was their early crisis. In year one Lucy worked about two days a week and he worked about three hours a day, expecting a "three hours a day and make millions" outcome. When he saw it failing he pushed harder, while Lucy kept other commitments (teaching design, radio show, writing novels). They had to explicitly decide to both go full time.
- Work-style differences: Lucy uses long task lists and meets deadlines; he focuses on habits and treats goals as "a carrot in front of a donkey," often missing deadlines. He lost interest before merging her finished work into production. His fix: ship what you did this week, and don't move on until it's shipped.

chunks.heading: Why they kept going when it wasn't working
chunks.text:
- They started logology after seeing a logo generator making money and assuming "we can do better because we have better logos." He calls this looking at one dimension of a successful startup and thinking you can beat it there. They were weak at marketing, validation and process.
- After about two years they had spent a third of their savings and made around $70 a month. He chose to go all in, spending down to the last roughly 10K, keeping enough runway to find a job.
- His motivation was the alternative: he didn't want to return to client work or a job, so "it's still better than the alternative."
- For a few months they had "literally no idea" how to succeed and kept trying anyway.
- Hard events stacked up: his mom died two months after they decided to build logology, the co-founder split got ugly, and money stress followed. He lost motivation after about two years, for the first time in his life, and developed insomnia.

chunks.heading: Perfectionism: where it hurt and where it paid off
chunks.text:
- Wasted perfectionism: roughly six months spent reinventing the tech stack and "the wheel for everything." He says the tech stack doesn't matter.
- Useful perfectionism: Lucy refused to compromise on logo quality. Feedback consistently included people saying it beat everything else, because a designer crafted each logo rather than a random database.
- A strong landing page also gave people a reason to check the product out. He doesn't claim it's the optimal way to get to market.

chunks.heading: How logology works and where it's headed
chunks.text:
- Lucy has designed more than 800 logos by hand; users get logos generated from her pre-made designs. Dagobert estimates 2,000 as the minimum for a good answer for anyone and 5,000 as ideal. Early focus was startups/tech; food and hair salons need more designs.
- They aim for timeless designs that last "100 years," not trends. Lucy dreams of publishing a book of her designs.
- Logology reached about $3K per month using Twitter and other marketing, with SEO work in progress.
- Insight from the course launch: people don't care about logos as much as the whole brand. The direction is to offer logos plus illustrations and a full vibe for buttons, navigation and landing pages ("Logology 2").

chunks.heading: Twitter as acquisition: authentic but strategic
chunks.text:
- He doesn't tweet about design because Lucy is the expert. Since his target market is startup founders, talking about his own startup journey makes them curious enough to check out the product. Some story tweets sent around a thousand people to his profile.
- This suits him because he dislikes feeling salesy ("I'm always shaking when I promote").
- Content process:
  - Step zero: engage with other people first; replies produce the best ideas.
  - Step one: turn the best replies into tweets. He built a make.com automation that pulls his most-liked replies from the past week and turns them into tweet drafts.
  - Step two: turn tweets into memes. He has made over 400 meme templates and posts about one per day.
  - Batch day: one or two days a month he spends 2-4 hours screenshotting about 100 meme templates from Reddit, 9GAG and other sites, then makes about 30 memes for the month.
- He says he mixes "authenticity with strategy." "Just posting whatever I want" is often a cop-out that avoids work that could fail.
- Being helpful is both real and strategic: it builds a brand as "someone nice who isn't trying to sell." His rule: "selfless in the morning and selfish in the evening" (engage with others' content in the morning, promote his own at night).
- He frames authenticity as a mix of selfless and selfish. You need to take care of yourself first to help others, and supporting other course creators (like Daniel Vassallo) also helps your own position.

chunks.heading: Twitter and mental health
chunks.text:
- Engaging on Twitter every morning pulls him out of his own head, since he's thinking about others' stories, and he reliably feels better afterward. It replaced the isolation of working alone.
- Seeing successful people can inspire him, or crush him in the wrong dose. He advises focusing on your own progress and not comparing, since you don't know others' full stories.

chunks.heading: Lesson: start with an audience and their problems, not a product
chunks.text:
- Logology was built the "genius idea first" way: build, then ask who to sell it to, then build an audience. His Twitter launch course was the opposite and worked far better.
- Course process:
  1. Build an audience on Twitter.
  2. Send tips by DM and learn what people need.
  3. Ask more precise questions about what they want to know.
  4. Write and iterate the landing page copy before building anything.
  5. Build the course, share early access, collect feedback, improve, release.
- Course revenue was easier partly because courses sell more easily, but he says part of the gap came from the process.
- Plan for Logology 2: start from his audience's problems, design the landing page and copy first, and only build once it's appealing.
- His summary: "Stop thinking of products, start thinking of audiences, people you care about, people you want to help," then build credibility and build what they want.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert explains how he built and launched his Twitter course after growing his audience, covering validation via the landing page, a pre-built launch list, and a Black Friday retweet-for-discount mechanic. He also shares his view on pricing, perceived value, and preparing for platform risk.

chunks.heading: How Dagobert built and validated the Twitter course
chunks.text:
Dagobert's Twitter course came from the same process he'd use for a SaaS: find the problems first, then build.

- He wrote the landing page before recording anything, to test whether the course could be engaging and solve a big problem.
- He asked his Twitter audience about their main problem with Twitter and compiled the answers into the value props.
- Core problems he targeted: people don't understand why they get no engagement, they waste time on Twitter, and they can't come up with tweets. So the course has an engagement section, a time routine, and a writing framework.
- His rule: "focus on problems, find two or three core features", exactly as he would for software.
- He first planned a book, spent a month writing it in Lisbon, and found each chapter took two days to make good. A friend suggested video because it tolerates more mistakes.

chunks.heading: Production process and cost
chunks.text:
- Five months of full-time work on the course and nothing else.
- Unscripted on purpose, to avoid sounding robotic: he worked from an outline of 23 chapters in the extended version. Each chapter took about two hours of takes.
- Over 30 hours of footage and about 60 hours of editing, a first for him.
- He spent a week watching about 30 hours of YouTube on lighting and sound.
- Gear cost about 500 dollars: three or four lights, three stands, a big sheet of paper for the background, t-shirts. He filmed on an iPhone rather than buy a 2K camera, since a failure would have cost too much.
- Work rate ramped from about 32 hours in week one to over 70 hours a week for two straight weeks before launch.
- Reception: people say it's the most in-depth Twitter course they've taken, and word of mouth now drives sales.

chunks.heading: Launch playbook: relationships first, then ask
chunks.text:
- During the five months he replied to people whose Twitter questions he'd answered, offering to DM them when the course came out. That built a list of 150 people.
- He had a list of about 50 mid-to-large accounts he'd supported for a year. He DMed them a week before launch and again on launch day. He was "blown away" by how many retweeted.
- His explanation: "you just give give give give and then eventually you ask", and they say yes because you gave first.
- Early access: three weeks before launch he sold about 10 copies to hardcore followers and used their feedback to improve the course. He gave a few to bigger accounts for free.
- Timing: he launched the last week of October so a Black Friday promo would fall at least a month later. Closer than that, he feared full-price buyers would feel burned.
- Result: about 10K dollars in the first week. Then 5 to 20 sales a day through November.

chunks.heading: Black Friday mechanic
chunks.text:
- 40% off, plus another 20% off (60% total) if the buyer retweets the Black Friday tweet.
- The aim was engagement, since tweets with links get less reach.
- Result: about 30K dollars in November, roughly 10K+ in December, and about 3K in the first 12 days of January.
- Why he expected it to work: he ran a 50% Black Friday for Logology the year before. It created awareness, and sales stayed above normal at full price afterward. This year Logology made about 1,800 dollars in that week.
- Sales now run about 2 to 5 a day. He mails stickers to buyers, who tweet about them, which spreads the course.
- Main version costs 80 dollars. A cheaper compressed version exists, but about 99% of buyers take the big one.

chunks.heading: Why the course sold: traffic was already solved
chunks.text:
- Logology already got 5K to 10K+ visitors a month from his Twitter account.
- He knew creators like Daniel Vassallo and Arvid convert far more traffic with a course. So with a link in his pinned tweet and bio, a killer product on top of the same traffic should sell.
- He rejected the claim that courses only sell at launch: he gets steady monthly traffic to it, as with Logology.
- He saw his audience grow from about 5K followers to roughly 50K in under a year.
- His lesson for others: find what your audience needs and build it for them.

chunks.heading: Pricing, perception and what people pay for
chunks.text:
- Indians bought the course far more than they ever bought logos. He first thought Indians were cheap, but they just don't value logos. A logo is far from money. A Twitter course promises more audience and sales.
- His rule: "the closer you are to the money, the higher the value". Communities and logos feel far from money. Sponsoring a podcast whose listeners buy your product feels close to it.
- Courses sell partly on the feeling of progress. Buying already feels like moving toward the goal, even if the buyer never watches.
- Design test he proposed: does your product let someone feel they gain something even if they buy it and never use it? Example: he paid 300 dollars for a one-time-fee maker community because it put him near successful makers, then left after a couple of months.
- He estimates a logo is seven times harder to sell than a Twitter course. French customers are the hardest to convert.
- Idea for Logology: sell a guide to designing a whole startup identity, something people feel they'll always need.

chunks.heading: Treating the course as a product
chunks.text:
