- He treats it like a SaaS with long-term updates. Plan: a new video (about 20 minutes) a few times a year on algorithm changes and what to change in your strategy. He sends free updates and bonuses.
- Gumroad stays his platform despite roughly 8% plus fees:
  - It handles affiliates (over 5K dollars from affiliates out of about 50K at the time).
  - It also handles newsletters, file delivery and updates, and visible ratings.
  - Its Discover section brings 2 to 3% of his sales.
  - He sees the fee like Stripe's 3% on Logology, as a convenience cost.
- Ratings: about 88 of 90 are five stars. Complaints are rare.
- Success case: Kyle was stuck at a couple thousand followers for years. After applying the course his impressions and startup sales rose about 4x and he neared 10K followers.

chunks.heading: Twitter risk, breaks and staying flexible
chunks.text:
- He takes breaks: he hadn't tweeted for four days at the time. He says that after a break you lose some reach because others filled the gap, so he spends extra time reconnecting when he returns.
- He now needs about two hours a day on Twitter, down from 10 hours when he started.
- Twitter is a "public square", not an email list. Impressions reach followers plus strangers.
- He doesn't plan a newsletter backup. He prefers the conversation on Twitter and is comfortable with uncertainty after years on Logology.
- He expects Twitter to keep improving under Elon Musk and cites the removal of nft spam bots.
- Business mindset: "everything will end eventually." Build savings and keep learning. The skills (courses, audience building) transfer to any platform. At the time the course revenue covered about a year of full salary, and he didn't feel they'd "made it".
- Logology is not abandoned. He wants to grow it to at least 10K a month and later teach that.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert, co-founder of Logology (automated designer-quality logos for startups), talks about bootstrapping on savings after 18 months of building and ~5 sales a month. He explains how a spammy tweet led him to Twitter and the daily interaction routine that grew his audience, plus lessons on branding, pricing tiers and signup friction.

chunks.heading: Starting out: building websites from age 15
chunks.text:
- Dagobert started building websites at 15, initially wanting to make video games. He joined a small teenage team that needed a website, and the feeling of turning an idea into something people could use got him hooked.
- He learned PHP from a free French tutorial site. After about three months of struggling and copying tutorials, a loop finally clicked: "it's kind of riding a bike". He was still a noob afterwards but could now build anything.
- His first money came at 16 from a fan site for the French Idol TV show. He bought the domain people would search for and offered the show's videos as free downloads, with an ad placed directly next to the download links (zero pixel margin) so many visitors clicked it by mistake.
- Results: about $150 in one night (the final), around $1,500 over a few months.
- The next season he built separate sites for every candidate, with comments and ratings. The TV channel's hosting provider shut it down once the channel launched its own online video platform, and he took everything offline.

chunks.heading: Freelancing, jobs and the pull toward his own thing
chunks.text:
- He left college after about a month, having already made about $2,000 from a single website.
- He freelanced for most of his professional life: web design, engineering, and mostly SEO on the marketing side. Early on he was paid very little, later thousands of dollars per site.
- Freelancing let him work directly with founders and find the ones he liked. Two examples:
  - A year in Moscow at 20 for a client building an e-commerce site.
  - A year helping a US friend build a social network startup.
- Bored of restarting with new clients, he chased money instead. He set a goal of a $100k/year US job. That also got boring.
- His realization: at 16 with the Idol site he already had what he wanted (own project, own terms, fun, money as a bonus). He had been chasing money instead of that.
- He says working for others always lacked something: "it's not your vision". Employment also spares you the anxiety of figuring it out yourself, which is the trade-off.
- He wanted to speak freely instead of being "a bit fake" for clients, and left jobs because managers blocked his attempts to build his own features.

chunks.heading: Logology: what it is and why it works
chunks.text:
- Logology gives a startup a designer-quality logo in about five minutes. It was co-founded with his wife, a graphic designer who did logos for 15+ years. Her custom logos cost around 3,000 euros, and many startup founders loved her style but could not afford it.
- Flow:
  - A roughly 5-minute questionnaire mirrors the questions she would ask a client (vision, values, target audience, industry, "which movie/superhero is your brand").
  - It outputs a brand personality (about 10 types, such as visionary, kind, playful).
  - It matches the user to logos from the 750+ she has designed.
- Pricing history: they first planned unique, one-time logos but that would need about $500 per logo. Customers said they would just hire a designer at that price. They moved to about $100, with packages from $50 and a $15 entry price mentioned at the end.
- Logos are licensed from a catalog, so another customer could in theory get the same one (he says it happens very rarely).
- Upgrade path: come back later and pay only the difference to get a unique version. Lucy spends an hour on the phone customizing it, so it can be trademarked.
- He argues customers who value branding see even $100 as cheap. Nobody from the US or Europe called it too expensive, and some said he should charge more. A testimonial from a well-known indie hacker said it was better than a 400-euro custom designer.
- Copying risk: they cannot stop screenshots, and a watermark would "kill the experience". Their protection is that a logo is public, so a thief is exposed, and they show the copyright and could sue.

chunks.heading: Branding for small startups
chunks.text:
- He agrees you do not need great branding to succeed. Google, Facebook, YouTube and Hacker News all started ugly.
- But those had revolutionary products. A small indie product usually does not, and people give you about five seconds, so he recommends a clear message, a fast site, a decent logo and consistent branding.
- A good brand gives the founder confidence and an edge. His landing page design draws compliments and makes visitors trust them quickly.
- Observation: the earlier Facebook example, slow app for years, only worked because Facebook was Facebook.

chunks.heading: The cost of bootstrapping and what keeps him going
chunks.text:
- Both he and his wife quit their jobs. They are living on savings: about $80,000 down over three years, around two days of vacation in three years, and a father-in-law who wants him to get a job.
- Timeline: spent 6 months deciding what to build, launched in early May 2021 after about 18 months, then sat at roughly five sales a month for a year. They need about 60.
- He passed 150 customers at the time of the interview.
- Early traffic came from friends, Reddit, Indie Hackers and startup directories. A big early mistake was requiring signup before showing any logos. Removing it produced the first real sales.
- What keeps him going is not confidence ("confidence will leave you") but something closer to faith. One sale a month plus a customer saying they love it is enough to feel "it's not hopeless".
- Paid tests that failed: Google Ads (~$500-600), a newsletter sponsorship ($200) and Reddit ads ($100), all with zero sales.

chunks.heading: The Twitter breakthrough
chunks.text:
- In late May he was desperate, so he searched Twitter for "what are you working on" style posts and replied with his link. With about 180 followers, one reply got around 100 clicks in 24 hours and 2-3 sales.
- A second viral post came from posting a screenshot of the creepy "I'll screenshot your logo" chat. That led to DMs with big indie hackers, including Arvid Kahl.
- He then put roughly 99% of his time into Twitter for three months and went from about 200 followers (June) to nearly 4,000, aiming for 10,000 by year end.
- His core rule: spend about 10 times more time interacting with other people's content than on his own tweets. After a viral post, he found that replying only on his own thread made the next day's tweets get no reach.
- Daily routine:
  - Morning: open the feed on "latest" (not the algorithmic view), scroll back to where he stopped last night, like and comment on lots of tweets (about 30 comments in an hour and a half), then reply to all his notifications.
  - Two scheduled tweets a day: one text, one meme.
  - Evening (around 9 pm): repeat the same interaction round.
  - About three hours a day total.
- Why it works, per him: when you interact with someone, their content and yours tend to show up in each other's feeds within 24-72 hours, and more interaction raises the ranking.
- He follows only about 250 people and wants real connections, so he does not outsource it. He notes that Twitter beats Instagram for conversion because people can click the profile link easily (a friend gets about 10x fewer link clicks from Instagram for similar views).

chunks.heading: Marketing mindset
chunks.text:
- He says marketing still feels mysterious: with programming he felt he could build anything after three months, but with marketing he cannot see how traffic maps to sales.
- He dislikes optimizing for algorithms rather than users, but accepts it as the cost of using social platforms.
- Spamming tweets as a last resort felt wrong, and he describes it as having "nothing to lose".
- Social media warps founder self-image: headlines about $30k MRR in a year teach nothing, and he used to feel like a failure for not making millions in two years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert explains how he grew a startup audience on Twitter by sharing his journey instead of promoting his product, then used the same emotional playbook to launch a crowded-niche course. He covers aggressive positioning, a pain-to-relief sales page, building the product after the landing page, and researching pains instead of ideas.

chunks.heading: Selling a Twitter course in a crowded market: positioning, emotion and pre-built promises
chunks.text: Dagobert is a software engineer who left a $100K job to bootstrap a startup with his wife, a designer. The startup is Logology, a website that generates logos automatically. They spent years and almost all their savings on it. The product wasn't the main problem. Marketing was, and neither of them is a marketer. He still sees himself as a startup founder first. The course is a side project that could bring in cash while they work on the startup.

chunks.heading: Why sharing his journey beat promoting the product
chunks.text:
- He first spammed his product link on Twitter, replying to people who needed a logo. It brought a couple of sales and little else.
- He then switched to sharing his founder journey, which is relatable to his customers (other startup founders). He didn't talk about logos, because his wife is the logo expert, not him.
- His reasoning is about volume. A product tweet might get 10 likes and 30 visitors. A story tweet gets 10 to 100 times the engagement and followers. Even if only 1% check out the product out of curiosity, that is far more people.
- His first viral tweet was a screenshot of a live chat in which a visitor said "I just stole one of your logos". Startup founders rallied behind him, he gained many followers, and it led to a logo sale.
- His conclusion: "most important thing is the emotion", because emotion is what gets engagement and action.
- With 50K+ followers, he still mentions the product only once or twice a month, for big milestones or features.
- He says the memes are low-touch and sell less directly, but laughter builds instant trust and goodwill. They make a large-scale audience feel like a personal connection.
- He advises choosing the format that is natural to you (jokes, visuals, expert threads). Authenticity is rare on social media, so genuine content gets attention.

chunks.heading: How he learned Twitter
chunks.text:
- At that point he made about $300 a month and had a Twitter following of about 150, mostly inactive school friends.
- He spent 8 to 10 hours a day on Twitter for about six months, including weekends.
- He ran many experiments on posting frequency, engagement and content. He deliberately tweeted good tweets at bad times to test his timing theory.
- After about two months he started to see the pattern. After about four months he had a repeatable daily process.

chunks.heading: Positioning the course against a saturated market
chunks.text:
- He avoided courses at first. He distrusts most course sellers, assuming they know only that courses make money.
- He changed his mind after helping people in DMs who asked how his small account took off. That showed him the value was real.
- Competitors included big names (he mentions Daniel Rosalo and Avid), with some courses reportedly making around $200K in a year. People in communities told him a course wasn't worth doing.
- His edge was a mix of strategic growth and authentic connection. Most courses offer only one: "be authentic" without growth, or hacky growth tactics without connection.
- Few competitors had a strong marketing position. Some had only a Gumroad page, so there was room to stand out.
- He named it "Dominate Twitter". In a poll of three titles, "Winning the Twitter feed" got the most votes. But those who chose "Dominate" felt strongly about it, while nobody loved the winner. Others called it too aggressive.
- He went with the polarizing name. His rule: "if I don't stand out I'm dead", and a strong emotional reaction beats a mild approval.
- His goal for the name was to get people to open the landing page, even if they thought they would hate it. The page then does the convincing.
- His wife's branding (strong black and white, a bold font) supports the aggressive tone, balanced with humor.

chunks.heading: The emotional sales page
chunks.text:
- He started designing the landing page before recording the course. He wrote about four versions first.
- He monitored Twitter complaints. The recurring pains were not understanding the algorithm, invisible tweets, and watching worse content go viral.
- The page follows an emotional arc:
  1. Push on the pain: you fail, you have zero engagement, people make fun of you (including a meme of someone tweeting daily with no result).
  2. Relief: it's not your fault, it's the algorithm.
  3. The way out: understand the algorithm and the pain goes away, via the course.
- His credibility comes from the algorithm. People in DMs told him he knows it better than anyone, so he built the course around it.
- An earlier headline was "the algorithm is killing your growth". He later changed it to a benefit-focused title about growing your startup with Twitter. He wants to A/B test the pain version again, since it opens with pain and emotion.

chunks.heading: Build the promise first, then the product
chunks.text:
- He did not pre-sell. DMs and competitors' sales were enough validation, and he was confident in the page.
- He designed the course to fulfill the landing page. He asked what chapters would make the page's promise true. For example, he added a tweet-writing section he hadn't planned, after hearing it was a pain point.
- Results: $8,073.30 in the first 24 hours, 700+ buyers and five-star reviews. Because it delivers on the promise, he now gets word-of-mouth sales as well.
- He contrasts this with the usual order of building the course (camera, lighting, months of recording) and then looking for reasons to sell it. He calls his approach about 10 times more effective.
- He is applying it to Logology: rebuilding from scratch by asking Twitter about branding and design pain, writing a landing page as strong as the course's, and then building the product to match.

chunks.heading: Market research without a big audience
chunks.text:
- Start with an industry or topic you care about (for him, design for startups), not a fixed product idea. This keeps you authentic and open to better ideas. He notes the real pain in his niche is how to design everything for a startup, not logos specifically.
- With few followers, monitor Twitter and Reddit communities for recurring problems. Twitter polls get extra visibility even on small accounts, though closed questions are less useful.
- With a large audience, he asks his audience and customers directly.
- Ask about pain, not ideas: "don't ask people what's your idea, ask people what's your pain". Ideas are casual and cheap. Real pain gets honest answers.
- About 20 in-depth conversations with people in the target market are enough.
- To validate, put up a landing page with a buy button and an early-access discount. Sales prove the pain is strong enough. His summary: "if there's pain there's money".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf explains how he and his designer wife automated a $3,000 branding service into a roughly $100 logo product, and how Twitter (spam plugs, then personal story and memes) turned about one sale a week into six or seven. He also covers listening only to paying customers, staying focused on marketing over features, and building instead of reading.

chunks.heading: Why Dagobert left a dream job to build Logology
chunks.text:
- At 15 he taught himself web development. He freelanced as a designer and engineer for almost 10 years.
- At 28 he got his "dream job" as a senior front-end engineer: remote, US salary, good team. After a couple of months he felt it was "the end of everything", with no more challenge.
- He concluded that what he loves is "the challenge" and "the adventure". Starting a company was the only thing left that excited him, even though he never wanted the stress and risk.
- Three years in, he says he still has trouble sleeping and is uncomfortable. But he hasn't been bored once, and he has "grown way more than in the eight years before".
- He argues many people stay stuck in jobs they dislike because they fear doing something else.

chunks.heading: How Logology came about
chunks.text:
- His first startup idea was "WordPress for mobile apps". He couldn't find anyone interested and lost energy after a couple of months.
- While on his honeymoon he saw on Indie Hackers a founder making good money with an automated logo service. He and his wife (a logo designer) had had the same idea about four years earlier. Back then they never assumed people would pay.
- She was also bored of 10 years of freelancing. They decided to build it, with "no plan", just the skills: she does logos, he does websites.
- He saw existing logo generators as doing a poor job. They make the user pick the symbol, font and color, so no designer is really involved.

chunks.heading: Product design: automating a $3,000 designer workflow
chunks.text:
- His wife charges about $3,000 for a custom brand. She had to turn away many prospects who only had about $200.
- Her real process has three steps: a workshop on values, vision and customers; five design proposals; then the client picks one and she finalizes it. Logology automates each step.
  - **Workshop becomes a quiz.** It is a five-minute "personality quiz" for your brand, with questions like "if your company was a superhero, which one would it be?". It does not ask "blue or red?". It assigns one of 10 pre-designed brand personalities.
  - **Proposals become pre-designed logos.** His wife designed about 700 logos by hand over three years. The tool matches roughly 30 of them to the user's personality and industry.
  - **Finalizing becomes curated choices.** Colors and fonts are hand-picked by her.
- Because every path was vetted by the designer in advance, "you can't go out of Logology with a shitty looking logo".
- One repeat customer bought five or more logos in a year. He now takes the quiz and picks a logo in about 20 minutes.
- A key customer testimonial says it is quick, affordable and high quality, the three things you're "not supposed to have together".

chunks.heading: Positioning, niche and pricing
chunks.text:
- He deliberately targets startups and indie founders, mostly SaaS and online products. Making the logos takes so long that they had to pick one vertical. Startups are likely to try something new and are easy for him to reach because they are like him.
- He plans to expand later to other businesses (hair salons, car mechanics).
- Main logo package: $100. Average revenue is about $70 per sale. He had about 200 sales at the time.
- Planned roadmap, each step building on the last:
  1. Logo only (today).
  2. A full brand guide (fonts, colors, spacing, dark mode, how to use the logo), planned at about $100. Early adopters already asked for it, and one paid for early access.
  3. Generated assets: social posts, landing page design, pitch deck templates. About $200 for everything, or possibly a subscription.
- Together, steps 1 and 2 would be about $200 per customer, so he could double revenue per customer.
- He sees "branding" as seen as something only for big companies. His hope is to make a real brand identity available to anyone with $50-100, and perhaps become a "branding API" that tools like Canva could plug into. He says the market is "still one step ahead".

chunks.heading: From 20 months of slow launch to growth on Twitter
chunks.text:
- It took 20 months to launch. Then more than a year to reach 100 sales, about five sales a month. He says they "didn't do good marketing" and had no idea how.
- What kept them going: early customers said Logology saved them, and he knew from his local entrepreneur circle that many others would care. He accepts that most people don't care about branding, and argues a small, well-defined audience that does is enough.
- Failed channels: Google Ads, sponsored newsletters, Indie Hackers posts (a few sales).
- Turning point (around May 2022): he started replying to "what are you working on?" tweets with Logology, about 20 times a day. One reply went viral, sending about 1,000 visitors in a day and a couple of sales.
- He dropped Reddit and Indie Hackers and focused on Twitter. He spent about 10 hours a day on it, reading guides, tweeting daily and sharing his founder story.
- Tweeting only to grow felt inauthentic and disconnected. So he also posted memes, since he is "the guy at parties who makes jokes". The memes took months to gain traction, but they now bring more people to his profile and website.
- Result: sales went from about one per week to about six or seven per week from Twitter alone. Monthly revenue was about $2,000-2,500. Followers were about 9,000, and he expected about 40k in 12 months at that rate.
- He now gets tagged whenever someone asks for a logo.

chunks.heading: Focus, feedback and priorities
chunks.text:
- **Listen only to paying customers.** People who didn't buy kept suggesting things like showing all logos in a catalog. Buyers want the opposite: "even less choice", more guidance. Following non-buyers would turn the product into a "stupid catalog" and lose the people who pay.
- **Marketing before features.** His priority is to survive and make a living, so he forces himself to keep focusing on marketing rather than building features. He builds new things only when he has spare room, such as a week with posts already written.
- **Stay focused.** He turns down unrelated ideas. They always seem easy and then bring unexpected problems, leaving "two weak products instead of one strong one".
- **A related side project:** "Memeology", a website collecting all his memes so people can reuse them. He sees it as another way to feed traffic to Logology.
- **Stop consuming, start building.** He used to read many books and built nothing. Now he says to stop reading and learn from experience, because real situations differ from what books describe.
  - His influences are Peter Thiel and the Basecamp founders (the "It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work" and "Rework" authors; he mentions a book on remote work), plus a few Twitter friends such as Tony Dinh.
- **Advice to his younger self:** set aside about two months, or even a few weeks, to build something you think is cool, and try to get one customer. Don't over-analyze market size. It teaches more than anything else and shows how different reality is from imagination.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert explains how a startup that failed on "build it and they will come" found its only working channel in Twitter. He covers the reply-first growth method, why authenticity beats AI-copied tweets, using memes to build trust, and why founders should market as a person rather than as a company.

chunks.heading: Starting a startup after hitting a wall in a job
chunks.text:
- Dagobert built websites from age 15 and worked as a developer, freelancer and consultant for years, often partnering with founders. Around age 28 he concluded the only remaining option for freedom and self-expression was building his own company, which he had avoided because it looked stressful and overwhelming.
- He quit his job as a software engineer for a US company (working remotely from France) with some savings and no firm idea.
- With his wife, who also wanted to stop freelancing, he spent a bit more than a year building Logology, then launched to nobody. They had assumed "building a good product would be enough" and neither was good at marketing.
- He argues that unless you build "the next Facebook," a product will not take off by itself; if you are not putting eyes on it, nobody cares.

chunks.heading: Finding Twitter after other channels failed
chunks.text:
- After the launch, he and his wife spent months and years trying Google Ads, sponsoring newsletters and writing blog posts. None worked.
- Out of desperation he began replying to tweets and promoting his startup with almost no followers. After a couple of weeks, one reply produced a few sales and visits. At the time Logology struggled to make more than one or two sales per week, so two sales in a day was big.
- Since everything else had failed, he went all in on Twitter.

chunks.heading: How Twitter scaled, and what it brought beyond sales
chunks.text:
- Unlike blogging, Twitter scaled roughly linearly for him: more followers meant proportionally more sales.
- Working Twitter basically full time for about three months took Logology from roughly 300-500 sales per month to about 2K, later stabilizing around 3K per month directly from Twitter.
- Side effects he values: podcast invitations, articles written about the company, and a PR effect he says he would not know how to do deliberately.
- SEO benefit: hundreds of websites now mention Logology because they found him on Twitter and liked his story.
- He calls Twitter "as much content marketing as it is networking" and says networking makes partnerships and problem-solving "10 times easier."

chunks.heading: Getting from 0 to 1,000 followers
chunks.text:
- He says zero to 1,000 is the hardest stretch; after that, social proof and engagement create momentum. Under 100 followers is hardest of all.
- The common mistake: tweeting daily to nobody. With no audience to like and propagate your tweets, "you might be hiding the best tweets in the world" and still get nothing.
- His switch: early on, spend time connecting rather than tweeting. Reply to and add value on tweets from people in your niche.
- Why replies work: on Twitter, a reply is as valuable as a standalone tweet and can go viral the same way, unlike a comment on YouTube or Instagram. Replying to people who already have an audience gets your content seen.
- Target accounts with a few hundred to a few thousand followers, not millions.
- Routine: about 30 minutes a day finding people who inspire you in your niche and engaging with their posts. He says this is usually enough to reach 500-1,000 followers. As you grow, shift more time to your own tweets.
- Proof of his own approach: he started about a year and a half earlier with around 100 followers and reached about 60K.

chunks.heading: Why he avoids AI tweets and copied viral content
chunks.text:
- He considers tools that resurface successful tweets from big accounts for you to lightly reword "pretty unethical," and says they fail for two reasons: copying content does not work without an audience, and it builds the wrong audience.
- He has seen accounts that started alongside him and grew faster (some over 200-300K) with viral lists, threads and recycled ideas. When those people later tweet about their own product or interests, they get almost no engagement because followers came for information, not for a human connection.
- His sales and opportunities come because his tweets are real. Some of his tweets still fail, because he keeps sharing his own thoughts and refining his thinking.
- On follower count: "between two times more and ten times more it doesn't change much, what matters is how many people care."
- ChatGPT can help match your voice, but the thoughts must be yours.

chunks.heading: Using Twitter as a founder: personal brand over company account
chunks.text:
- He argues Twitter is about people. People would follow Steve Jobs over Apple, Elon Musk has far more followers than Tesla or SpaceX, and LeBron James has more than the Lakers.
- Best use for a CEO: connect directly and remove the distance marketing creates. A founder talking about building a product is more emotional than an ad or a brand account.
- He admits many CEOs want "easy marketing that scales" (set a budget, click a button, get a return) and says Twitter does not work that way; the payoff is trust and authority as a person in your niche, which then boosts anything you build.
- His Twitter view after Elon Musk's takeover: he launched his Twitter course the day Musk took over and was stressed, but found the changes smaller than announced. He cites bot fixes (he had been getting three NFT-scam bots tagging him daily until they fixed it) and says he avoids following Musk to protect his peace.

chunks.heading: Memes as a trust-building tool
chunks.text:
- Memes connect emotionally: laughter creates trust. Humor alone makes people trust you but not take you seriously, so he balances memes with valuable content that shows he knows his field.
- He has made 400+ memes over more than a year, aiming for one per day, as a self-imposed challenge. Each takes about 30 minutes on average. It became what people know him for.
- Process: the image matters most. "If it's funny by itself you already won half." He initially used mediocre images with jokes and it did not land.
- Find images on meme sites such as 9GAG and Reddit until one is very funny, then adapt it to your niche.
- Content angles: (1) make fun of a real pain your audience shares (for him, startup founders), turning a tough situation into a joke; (2) deliver a simple truth in a light way, such as his repeated lesson that founders need to do more marketing, not just build a product.

chunks.heading: Persisting through three years without income
chunks.text:
- He originally expected to make millions. After years of struggle, goals became realistic: just making a good living.
- After about two years they had spent roughly half their savings and nearly quit, then decided to commit fully rather than go back to the work they no longer wanted.
- His reason to continue: nowhere to go back to. "I'm not going back... this is the life I chose."
- He argues a deeper motivation than money is required, since money alone is quicker to earn with a job, savings and real estate.
- Advice on platforms: spreading across many platforms thins you out and makes real relationships harder. Pick one and stick with it; he stays on Twitter and rarely uses LinkedIn.
- At recording he said Logology was pivoting, with a goal of reaching 10K per month that year.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf explains how he and his designer wife turned a $2,000 custom logo service into a $100 automated questionnaire-to-logo product. He covers getting the first customer, when startups should invest in branding, and standing out in a crowded no-code market.

chunks.heading: Why Dagobert and his wife built Logology
chunks.text:
- Dagobert is a French developer who started in web development and design at 15. He later specialized in front-end engineering (React, JS) and worked for French, Russian and US companies.
- He describes himself as "pretty easily bored". After a job he liked, he asked "is that it?" and concluded he had "no other idea except to try" building his own company.
- The idea came on his honeymoon road trip through the US South. He and his wife, a designer, saw someone talk about success with a logo business and decided to build one. The idea dates to roughly three years before this October 2021 interview.
- His wife has designed logos for 10+ years, including for successful French startups. She charged about 2,000 euros per logo.
- Many people loved her work but had only about 200. She had to say no, or she wasted time on low-paid jobs.
- The insight: automate her process so the same quality costs about 100 dollars instead of 2,000.

chunks.heading: How Logology works
chunks.text:
- Logology is a website that generates logos. The logos are real designs, not icons pulled from a database.
- Dagobert's wife has designed more than 600 logos over roughly 2.5 years. The catalog is organized by startup industry (productivity apps, communication apps, cleantech, biotech, marketing and more), with logos meant to carry meaning for each.
- The flow copies how she works with clients. She asks about vision, values and target customer, then proposes ideas. Customers rarely say "do a bird", so the value is in what the designer brings.
- Users answer 11 questions, which take about 3-4 minutes. The questions are abstract, like "if your startup was a movie, what would it be?".
- Logology then matches the user with logos, fonts and colors and sells the result for about 100 dollars.
- It also describes the user's brand personality. Users say "that's me", and some told them to sell just that.
- Some users find the abstract questions off-putting. They are looking for ways to make it easier.
- They A/B test the homepage button text. They are cautious about testing the button color because their visual identity is strong.

chunks.heading: Getting the first customer
chunks.text:
- The first customer came a year before the interview, in late April, right after they announced the product. She was a loose acquaintance from a friend group.
- She came to the site, found "the logo I've always wanted", and bought it within hours.
- Dagobert's takeaway: the product is very good for a few people, who fall in love and buy instantly. The hard part is repeating that with everyone.
- He says a friend buying still counts, since it is still value exchanged for money.
- Early on they used FullStory session recordings to find UX problems and watched the first buyer's session live. He later removed it because it felt "very creepy" and made them stop working.

chunks.heading: When a startup should invest in a logo
chunks.text:
- He used to tell founders not to spend 2,000 on a logo when they have 10,000 to build the product, and to find profitability first.
- He still believes a startup shouldn't spend real money on a logo. That is why Logology is deliberately cheap rather than pivoting upmarket.
- But his view has shifted. Early internet products (Google, YouTube, Facebook) could win on innovation alone. Today, with no-code, "hundreds or even thousands of products" launch daily, and landing pages and logos all look the same.
- Branding is more important than 5-10 years ago for standing out. A distinctive brand gives people "a bit of a pause" instead of a skip.
- The product, copy and differentiation still matter, and may matter more.
- His rule of thumb: with zero customers, don't bother. Once you have about 10-20 people who love what you do, a logo is a useful next step.

chunks.heading: Tools and recommendations
chunks.text:
- Daily tool: Roam Research, for networked notes and connecting ideas (related to the Zettelkasten method).
- Books: "Zero to One" by Peter Thiel is his go-to. He also recommends April Dunford's "Obviously Awesome", which helped them figure out their positioning and the problem they had communicating the product.
- Indie hacker to watch: Danny Postma, who executes fast on varied ideas. One example was turning a landing page site into a tool for building landing pages from inspiring blocks.

chunks.heading: Marketing and audience
chunks.text:
- Dagobert says marketing is the one skill he and his wife lack, since between them they cover design and engineering. They are starting to learn it.
- He was very active on Twitter, mixing insight and humor. He forces himself to make memes to grow his account.
- His Twitter handle is dagorenouf, and the site is logology.co.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert explains how a failed paid-ads attempt pushed him to organic Twitter. He covers why Twitter has no reach ceiling, why personal story tweets beat memes and guru one-liners, and why a face-and-name account beats a brand account. He also covers engaging first to get shown and how a small audience can still pay off.

chunks.heading: From "good product" to realizing marketing was the problem
chunks.text:
- Dagobert was a software engineer and consultant who left a good job to build a startup with his wife. They expected to be profitable within a couple of years.
- Sales didn't come. Customers' feedback and his own conclusion, after a couple of years, was that the product wasn't the problem, marketing was.
- Neither he nor his wife saw themselves as marketers. He had to choose between quitting or doing marketing anyway, and he kept going until he found a channel that worked, which turned out to be Twitter.

chunks.heading: Paid and sponsored channels failed first
chunks.text:
- He assumed he could put money into Google Ads and get customers out, which he calls the dream of anyone who isn't into marketing.
- He spent $600 on Google Ads and got about 600 visits and zero sales. He found it humbling to see how much work it takes to convince people beyond buying clicks.
- Sponsoring newsletters also failed.
- That left organic reach. His reasoning was "I'm not going to keep paying, I have no choice."
- On Indie Hackers he found a voice, got on the front page a couple of times, and made a few sales. He then tested Indie Hackers, Reddit, product discussion boards and Twitter side by side.

chunks.heading: Why he picked Twitter over Indie Hackers
chunks.text:
- He started on Twitter about 10-11 months before this talk, purely to promote his link. He searched for "what are you working on today" and "Indie makers, what are you building" posts and found an excuse to mention his product.
- He expected social traffic to be low quality, but found it similar in quality to Indie Hackers traffic.
- One of those promo tweets got about 60 likes, 2 sales and roughly 1,000 visitors to his site.
- His main argument is that Twitter is an open system with no ceiling. A great Indie Hackers post tops out at about 3,000 views and maybe 500 visitors to his site. On Twitter, reach keeps growing as followers grow.
- Over time he saw fewer sales from Indie Hackers and more from Twitter, and chose to focus on Twitter.

chunks.heading: Measure the channel, don't over-optimize it
chunks.text:
- He tracked where each sale came from. Once he knew buyers came from his Twitter, he took that as proof the channel worked.
- He has lots of event tracking on his site but says "the simpler the better sometimes."
- He wasted a lot of time earlier overthinking tiny funnel optimizations that he hoped would double his conversion and that changed nothing.
- His view is to measure everything but not put too much hope in small optimizations, and to go partly on instinct.

chunks.heading: Story tweets beat one-liners and memes
chunks.text:
- **What failed:** he first tried to sound like a Twitter guru, writing polished one-liners like the ones he saw succeeding. Nobody engaged. He believes a good one-liner is very hard because every word has to be perfect, and you need real authority to pull it off.
- **What worked:** he stopped pretending to know everything and shared his own experience with more humility ("this happened to me today"). That is when traction began.
- **The format:** a "story tweet" of about five to six short lines separated by blank lines, usually with an emoji at the end of each line. It follows a short arc of context, problem, solution, then the emotional ups and downs and what he learned.
- **No product pitch:** he talks about his startup without naming it, so the takeaway reads as a universal lesson.
- **Results:** at around 1,000 followers, story tweets often got about 500 likes. One got 1,600 clicks to his profile and about 300 new followers.
- **Memes:** he makes them himself, and began making them for fun, not as a strategy. They typically got 30 to 100 likes. People laugh and keep scrolling without clicking his profile, so they convert far worse than story tweets, even though memes are what people mention when they describe him.

chunks.heading: What to share when building in public
chunks.text:
- A post needs a lesson learned or a strong emotion: excitement (for example a big sales day) or a hard day, as long as it isn't just depressing and gives people something to relate to or hope from.
- Most often he shares a lesson from something he went through.
- Turn a mundane update into a story: "Today I had this problem, I found this solution, and it gives me hope for X." A flat "I did this today" isn't useful to readers, but a problem-solution story lets them learn and recognize themselves in it.
- His rule: share what you went through, then what you got out of it and what you learned, so others can learn too.

chunks.heading: Personal account vs brand account
chunks.text:
- Both can work, but he recommends using your own face and name.
- His example: would you rather follow Apple or Steve Jobs? Most people say Jobs, because they want to hear from the visionary and not product updates.
- To build an emotional bond and turn people into fans who trust you and spread the word, people need someone they can relate to, which is much harder to do with a brand.
- Valid reasons to hold back include wanting anonymity or not wanting to mix in personal or political content.
- If that applies, he suggests starting a fresh account. He did this himself after years of not using an older, family-oriented account, and a dedicated startup account made it easier to be himself without mixing in personal topics.

chunks.heading: Getting likes: engage first, and you don't need a huge audience
chunks.text:
- **How the algorithm works:** your feed first shows people you have DMed, replied to or liked before. To get your tweets shown first to others, engage first with a handful of people you resonate with.
- **How to do it:** reply with value to their tweets, build a relationship and interact regularly. They will engage back, Twitter will show your content to them first, and your tweets get early likes and a chance to spread.
- **Be specific:** he agrees with advice to avoid random tweets. Pick a clear theme and post consistently.
- **Audience size:** you don't need millions of followers. He argues that the more followers someone has, the less successful they often are in business. Some people he once looked up to turned out to be struggling and broke.
- **What matters:** he says what matters is trust and deep connection with the right people, so that they buy when they need you. If you connect deeply enough, a small audience is sufficient, and it depends on your product and its price.
- **His own numbers:** he said he was making about $3K a month at the time. He attributed that to his product not being the best fit for his audience, not to a problem with the audience.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf (Logology founder) explains why big ambition causes perfectionism and how focusing on small goals gets him shipping. He covers why personal brands beat company accounts, why repeating content kills Twitter engagement, and why channels like affiliates need time before you judge them.

chunks.heading: Dagobert on handling uncertainty and spontaneity in content
chunks.text:
- He avoids scripting and recitation. For his Twitter course he records each chapter from a title and a few notes, talks for about 30 minutes, then cuts it later. He says scripted delivery "would feel like kind of dead," while spontaneous delivery carries energy and emotion.
- He deliberately avoids preparing for podcasts. When hosts send questions in advance, he purposely doesn't read them, because he wants to train himself to be spontaneous.
- He was inspired by Lil Wayne, who stopped hiding his lyrics and got better by doing hundreds of songs a year.
- He says he has more fun speaking English than French because it feels less serious and mistakes feel more forgivable.
- When cutting video, he plans to cut where he can show an image, so only the audio cuts and the edit isn't obvious.

chunks.heading: Big dreams, small goals, and why ambition causes procrastination
chunks.text:
- He started his startup (Logology) with his wife four years ago and says he got comfortable with uncertainty only recently.
- He realized he was procrastinating because a huge ambition creates a fantasy of what must be achieved. Since the outcome can't be guaranteed, he fell into perfectionism, reassuring himself by polishing tiny details for months.
- His fix: "keep having big dreams" but "focus on small goals." For the course, he would be legitimately happy selling "a couple dozen copies" to people he can help, and that mindset made recording possible.
- He gave the same advice to a founder (Shield) earning a couple hundred dollars a month who wondered whether to quit: try reaching the next goal, such as $500, then $1,000, then $10,000.
- He says dreaming can't fail, while doing always involves struggle, sometimes not even your fault (market, customers). But "when you're in it you have a chance to get better, so get in it as fast as possible."
- He still holds big dreams (1 million Twitter followers, a course making $50k in its first week) while accepting he doesn't control outcomes, and he stays grateful for the small steps.

chunks.heading: Too much consumed knowledge fuels perfectionism
chunks.text:
- He stopped reading books, listening to podcasts and reading most articles. In his 20s he consumed so much that "nothing was good enough" and nothing checked all the boxes he knew existed, which fed perfectionism and fear of launching.
- Too much information leaves him unsure which way to do things. He says it's time to start doing, experiment, and learn for yourself.
- He would read a book only when facing a very clear problem it could solve, not for reading that only confuses.

chunks.heading: Twitter growth: the novelty curve and refreshing your content
chunks.text:
- He went from about 150 followers in May 2021 to hundreds of thousands of people exposed, after a few months of figuring out the algorithm. He calls Twitter free, high-potential distribution that can expose you to people who don't know you, which a newsletter can't do.
- Growth curve: about 1,000 to 10,000 followers between September and December 2021 as "the hot new thing." Like fashion or a hit song, novelty fades and people get tired.
- His read on big accounts complaining about lost engagement: they repeat the same ideas for six months, so people get bored. He says he did the same, and the same joke told a hundred times gets less funny. He names Jack Dorsey as an example of someone with few likes relative to followers who doesn't complain.
- His response is "season two": new, deeper, more philosophical content still related to startups. In year one he spent hours a day thinking of content, then kept repeating it to capitalize on it.
- His Twitter course targets the first stage: getting your thoughts heard when "you tweet some things and nobody hears about them," via strategy and the algorithm. A possible later course would cover maintaining success.
- He expects waves: audiences come and go, algorithm changes shift content, and bad months pass. He ties this to startups ("there's a new wave coming up at some point").

chunks.heading: Twitter and newsletter work together
chunks.text:
- Twitter is for spreading ideas and reaching new people. Most followers are not fans; they saw something they liked and rarely return.
- A newsletter is a deeper, long-term relationship with real fans. People who complain about Twitter engagement often built large newsletters because of Twitter.
- He says you need both. He has no active newsletter beyond a product-specific one.
- He loves Twitter as a social space ("my own personal co-working space"), which is why he doesn't move to TikTok or LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: Acquisition channels: keep trying, don't get stuck
chunks.text:
- Twitter is his main acquisition channel, so lower reach cuts Logology sales. He is responding by starting SEO and trying more channels.
- Affiliates: he opened the product to affiliates about a year before this interview. For roughly a year it produced almost nothing and cost about $30 a month. In the last couple of months, 10 to 15 percent of sales came from affiliates (about $400 a month), because some affiliates finally found a good way to talk about the product.
- His rule: don't give up too soon (he could have stopped affiliates after three months), but don't stay stuck repeating what isn't working. "Keep doing different things."

chunks.heading: Personal brand versus company brand
chunks.text:
- He says it is about 10 times easier to build an audience for a person than for a brand. People want the founder, the vision and behind-the-scenes content (his example: you'd follow Elon Musk, not SpaceX product updates).
- Exceptions: if you plan to sell the startup, or run very different products in unrelated industries, a brand account makes more sense. If most of his traffic came from a Logology account, it would be easier to sell; his traffic comes from his personal account.
- If you build several products around one topic, he recommends a personal brand. He plans more products (a Twitter course, possibly others), all related to marketing and branding, which fits one audience.

chunks.heading: Small, enjoyable business versus chasing a unicorn; finding the middle on effort
chunks.text:
- Logology numbers: about $3K a month revenue against about $5K needed for two people, plus roughly two years of runway from savings. He says he is grateful not to have a job.
- He criticizes founders who earn enough but feel unhappy because they chase big lifestyles. He cites a solo founder making about $3,000 a month who pivoted after seeing competitors earn more, neglected the product, and lost Dagobert as a paying customer.
- He cites Peter Levels (about 60 products before one made millions) as an approach that works for some, but says he prefers a small business he enjoys. He thinks many "good enough" businesses never exist because people quit when they don't make millions in three months.
- On effort: he warns against both extremes. Perfectionism cost him about 20 months to launch plus nearly a year more to find real traction. A weekend launch that fails also avoids pain because there is no attachment.
- His advice: with some pre-validation, spend one to two months giving it "a real go," not perfectionist, then see how people react. For his course he spent about $400 on lights, a black background and a mic, using an iPhone instead of buying a camera.
- Both extremes avoid the pain of failure. He says embracing that pain is fuel to keep improving, and his Twitter course failing would hurt him.
- He says early confidence was arrogance based on fantasy. Real confidence comes after launching, failing and learning, like learning to swim by going in the water.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf explains how he turned Twitter into Logology's main marketing channel by connecting one-on-one and sharing his founder story. He also covers bootstrapping for freedom, automating his wife's design process into a product, and waiting to launch on Product Hunt until there is momentum.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping with a spouse: building Logology
chunks.text:
- Dagobert and his wife, an experienced logo designer, started Logology in September 2018. He had saved money from a software engineering job; she was a freelance brand consultant.
- The problem: startups came to her wanting a brand, but projects started around $3,000 and they only had $100-200. Her answer to them was "no solution".
- The idea was to automate her process into three steps:
  - A five-minute quiz that finds the brand personality. She used to do this in a one-day workshop with post-it notes.
  - Matching logos from a pre-designed library. She designed more than 700, after about 15 years of experience. Focusing on startups let them split the market into brand personalities and industries.
  - Customizing font and color within boundaries she set, so the result can't look ugly.
- He describes it as "an automated version of her". The wife does the creative work ahead of time and the product delivers it instantly.
- The name: the first choice, "Logo Stories", was already trademarked in France. After about three weeks of brainstorming they landed on "Logology" (the study of the meaning of symbols). They didn't like it at first, now love it.
- They bootstrap on purpose. They want to get rich, but mostly want freedom to work on their own terms, and he sees investors as a compromise.
- When money ran low, his wife took on occasional custom logo contracts, about one every two months, to keep them afloat while Logology grew. At the time of this interview they were close to profitability.
- Extras he mentions: saving the quiz process gives a free branding course (colors, symbols, fonts, casing) with five versions, one per brand personality. A guide on applying the brand beyond the logo was in progress.

chunks.heading: Growing on Twitter from 150 to 15,000+ followers in eight months
chunks.text:
- Context: after about three years, the product was good and people loved it, but almost nobody knew about it, so sales were near zero.
- He had tried ads, blogs and communities. A reply that went viral and brought a few sales pushed him to commit to Twitter, with "nothing else to lose".
- Eight months before the interview he had about 150 followers; at the interview, over 15k.
- His content: daily stories about his startup journey, plus memes. Memes started as fun for a few friends (his first got 2-3 likes) and later became video memes.
- The mistake he says many people make is treating Twitter "like a TED talk", broadcasting thoughts to the world. For a normal founder it's about one-on-one connection:
  - Visit people's profiles, look at what they post, engage constantly.
  - Connect authentically, not in a fake networking way. He sees Twitter as more relaxed than LinkedIn.
- Why it sells: startup founders are his target customers. They relate to his story, connect with him, and come to Logology when they need a logo.
- Party analogy: you don't skip hello and then say "come to my party tomorrow". Mingle first, plug your product when it's relevant.

chunks.heading: What counts as spam, and what to avoid on Twitter
chunks.text:
- Never use "Promote" on your tweets. Even paying $10 for reach is, in his view, a red flag, because viewers can no longer trust the likes and engagement were real.
- Spam is not binary. The same reply can be spam or value depending on context.
- Good: replying to a productivity tip with something that adds to the conversation, then mentioning your productivity app with some humility.
- Bad: dropping your crypto project link under tweets about startups.
- The test: is it relevant, is it humble, and are you adding value or just plugging?

chunks.heading: Why bootstrappers should focus on marketing and ignore big startup books
chunks.text:
- He read many startup books before launching (he names ideas like crossing the chasm, unfair advantage and big markets). He calls the concepts good but written for VC-funded startups.
- That advice assumes money to "throw a million dollars on Facebook ads" and run experiments. A tiny bootstrapped startup can't use it.
- He says there is very little material about starting when you are tiny and unfunded.
- His advice:
  - Experiment yourself.
  - Find communities of people like you.
  - Don't read too much into the big startup books, because they can make you overthink and try to answer questions you don't need to answer yet.
- His main tweeting theme is that founders should focus on marketing more than on product.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt strategy
chunks.text:
- He had not launched yet and says to take his view "with a grain of salt", based on watching friends launch.
- Two ways to launch:
  - Launch at the start to get first users and feedback. You may be disappointed by traction, but it kickstarts a new project.
  - Launch later, once you have a solid product, happy customers and some audience. His chosen approach.
- Why later: existing momentum can propel you to top spots of the day, and the push can go viral in a way that is nearly impossible without it.
- Follow-on benefits: the "product of the day" badge helps conversion, you can contact media, and the launch becomes part of your story for PR.
- His framing: Product Hunt is step two, not step one. Step one ("hey look at my product") fails because nobody knows you.

chunks.heading: Logo and branding opinions
chunks.text:
- Branding is about meaning, not just aesthetics. A logo should convey the company's values and story.
- Calendly's new logo: he disliked it. It's a blob that "doesn't mean anything", and he preferred the earlier simple calendar-with-a-C.
- Alphabet's logo: a plain one is fine because it's a holding company and not customer-facing, so marketing doesn't depend on it.
- Similar logos: every simple logo has probably been done somewhere, since there are limited shapes. What matters is whether two companies compete in the same space and cause customer confusion (a legal issue). The simpler the symbol, the likelier overlap, so the story around it matters more.
- Reading a logo: orange and pointy reads as aggressive and action-oriented. Good for coaching, wrong for baby diapers. An upward arrow signals progression and aspiration, and a dark corporate palette signals business.
- A designer's rule of thumb (his wife's view): a logo with too much detail breaks when shrunk onto a tiny sweater tag. Font weight should balance the symbol.

chunks.heading: Approach to new tech and crypto
chunks.text:
- He holds a small amount of crypto for fun, using money earned from it. He bought Bitcoin about five years earlier, it roughly 10x'd, and he sold enough to recover his original money.
- He admits he doesn't really understand crypto, but makes small bets so he doesn't miss out.
- In his 20s he jumped on every new technology. His current rule: ignore new tech at first, and if it is still in the news about three years later, pay attention. He says you aren't really late, because you are still early.
- On accepting crypto payments at Logology: no objection, but it needs implementation time and tax handling. He's focused on what helps customers and sales, and doesn't think crypto does yet.
- On adoption: businesses mostly aren't for it because he sees no clear problem it solves for them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf, co-founder of Logology, explains how he went from spamming "what are you building" threads to participating on Twitter, why organic beat paid for his bootstrapped startup, and how he automated a designer's service workflow into a product. He also covers staying motivated through hopeless stretches.

chunks.heading: Why Logology started: accessible branding for early-stage founders
chunks.text:
Dagobert co-founded Logology with his wife Lucie Baratte, a freelance logo designer of 10+ years, and he builds the product as the developer. The idea came on their honeymoon.

- Lucie kept hearing from founders who loved her style but could not pay about $3,000 for a custom logo ("I only have a hundred").
- The mission is to make professional brand design accessible to entrepreneurs at the earliest stage.
- Logology is not a logo generator. It adds brand advice and a design-thinking approach, so a customer gets a meaningful identity rather than a random icon. The site's meta description is "get your brand identity within five minutes".
- Every logo in the catalogue is designed by Lucie, who chose each color and font combination in advance. Logos are not randomly generated.

chunks.heading: Turning a service into a product (automation with a personal touch)
chunks.text:
- The first six months went nowhere because Dagobert and Lucie tried to design the product "in our heads". The fix was to copy exactly what Lucie does with her freelance clients and automate it.
- Lucie's method is design thinking applied to visual identity, run as interactive workshops that define the logo.
- Lucie wanted about 1,000 keywords so users could describe themselves precisely. Dagobert judged that too service-heavy to automate. They settled on roughly 10 brand personality types, mixed with the customer's industry.
- Lucie spent about a month writing the post-purchase branding-advice email sequence. It is tailored to the buyer's personality type, so the automation feels personal.
- Dagobert treats a $49 logo buyer like a former freelance client. They write handwritten cards and email every customer, and he is often on live chat.
- Both founders spent years in service work. They now want to build a product, which they find more fun and more valuable.
- A guest customer said the whole flow (questionnaire, color and font suggestions, follow-up emails, guidelines) is why he would pick Logology again over generators and freelance designers.

chunks.heading: From spammy promotion to "participating": how Dagobert approached marketing
chunks.text:
Dagobert held a bias against marketing for the first two and a half years, and Logology sold few logos. His reasoning is that marketers are often "bullshitters", so people picture something shady and salesy.

- He started by posting the product in every online community.
- On Twitter he searched for indie hackers and "build in public" people answering "what are you building today?". He replied "I'm working on Logology today" about ten times a day for weeks. He calls this spammy and low quality.
- The shift came from participating sincerely: listening, engaging and bringing value. People became curious about Logology on their own.
- His view: "Real marketing is about connecting with people, listening to people", and promoting the product only when it is useful.
- He says reframing marketing as participating also made it more fun and easier. He now calls himself more of a participant than a marketer.
- He considers early spamming a normal first step for most founders, because marketing is experimentation.

chunks.heading: Organic beats paid at this stage
chunks.text:
- In early 2021 Dagobert spent about $600 on Google Ads and got zero sales. Hundreds of people clicked, but nothing converted. Budget was limited, so they stopped.
- He also sponsored newsletters aimed at startup founders and indie hackers. That went nowhere either.
- Twitter then started working. Today almost all of Logology's sales trace back to Twitter, directly or indirectly.
- His reasoning: people have defenses against ads because they know you paid. When they see something they like from a person on Twitter, they trust it more.
- Retargeting ads to remind people who started a logo are a possible future test. He thinks getting paid ads right takes at least a few thousand dollars, and they do not want that risk yet.
- Lucie is now writing blog posts on design and branding to build a resource that can bring Google traffic, which is still organic.
- Dagobert acknowledges the tradeoff: when you have no money you invest time, and once you have money you can save time with it.

chunks.heading: Advice to first-time founders: pick work you enjoy and keep going
chunks.text:
- Dagobert says most founders expect to make millions because they have big ideas. When that does not happen they are disappointed, and that is where the real work starts.
- Positive motivation ("change the world") stops helping when you have no customers. In the hopeless stretch around 2021 he used negative motivation instead: "I don't want to go back to a job." He preferred to keep trying things until something worked than to return to work he wanted to avoid.
- His main advice is to build something you enjoy doing even if it fails. Lucie will always be happy designing logos, and he is happy building product and talking to founders on Twitter.
- If you only chase a "good idea", it starts to look like a bad idea the moment it gets hard. Enjoyment is what keeps you going until you "climb back up".
- Both founders stress mental health in the hard stretches. Lucie says a bad mental state "will shadow your vision". Dagobert suggests meditation, yoga, a therapist or a coach.
- Lucie's advice on marketing: stay genuine, talk to customers, and listen to their problems. Do not just do whatever they ask.

chunks.heading: Where Logology goes next
chunks.text:
- Lucie and Dagobert plan to rebalance between marketing and product after a period where Dagobert spent most of his time on marketing.
- The product will expand beyond logos to fuller brand identity: guidelines, more colors, more fonts and more files.
- They plan to introduce parity pricing across products.
- Lucie is writing blog articles on branding and on how customers can manage their brand and tell their story.
- Context: after about three years of work, Logology only became sustainable in the last six months before this interview (October 2022).
- Possible future direction: working with other designers and paying them fairly. Dagobert and Lucie say Logology is the only online logo solution built to pay designers fairly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: After 13 months averaging one user a week and failed paid channels, Dagobert went all-in on Twitter, sharing his struggles and memes. The community that formed recommended his product (even non-customers) and brought backlinks, partnerships and interviews. He also covers topic keywords, repurposing replies into tweets, and batch scheduling.

chunks.heading: Twitter as the only channel: authenticity over networking
chunks.text:
Dagobert Renouf co-founded Logology (logology.co), a logo generator for startups, built with his wife, who is an expert logo designer. For about 13 months it averaged one user per week. He turned it around by sharing his founder story on Twitter. His follower count went from under 100 to thousands within weeks, and he says revenue quadrupled.

- He describes himself as introverted and bad at traditional networking. On Twitter he doesn't try to network; he shares what he is going through.
- He argues authentic, vulnerable posts connect on a deeper level, even when some days get little engagement.
- Other founders identify with the struggles, so they come to care about him personally, not only the product.
- He contrasts this with "resource thread" accounts that grow to 100k followers but never connect on a human, personal, emotional level.

chunks.heading: Community turns into referrals, and many referrers never bought
chunks.text:
- Around August or September 2021, he saw someone ask for a logo designer and get about 30 replies. Nine of them recommended Logology, from people he didn't know and who weren't customers.
- He says nine out of ten people who recommend Logology never bought anything. They like him and what he is doing, so they recommend him.
- His view: the more vulnerable and authentic he is, the stronger the community gets. It works like friends supporting each other, so he also helps and supports other founders on Twitter.
- Kevin C.W. Hellon's tweet is the example: he thought of logology.co when someone asked for a logo because of Dagobert's consistent meme posting and presence.

chunks.heading: Content process: reply-first ideas, scheduling, and mixing tone
chunks.text:
- He builds a bank of ideas by engaging with others daily. Most tweets now start as a reply that got likes, which he calls "an MVP for my tweets", then repurposes as a standalone tweet because it is likely to do at least moderately well.
- He keeps his next 30 days of tweets written and scheduled.
- After a stretch of "brutal truth" memes about getting zero users and zero money, followers said it was too depressing. He now mixes the week: some painful or funny, some happy, some celebratory, some about how hard it is. He doesn't want to run all depressing content Monday to Friday.
- He is both very transparent in what he shares and strategic about how he uses Twitter.

chunks.heading: Memes and tools
chunks.text:
- Image memes: Imgflip (img-flip.com). He started with its templates and added his own captions. He likes Spongebob memes because they work well, not because he is a fan.
- Video memes: Pinata Farms, a kids' app with caption tech that tracks the character in a video. It is US-only. He switched his App Store region to California with a fake address (after cancelling his subscriptions) and downloaded it. When an update forced a redo, he contacted the team and they gave him the private TestFlight beta build.
- Scheduling: Hypefury, chosen because it was the first he heard of. He still pays for it. Many scheduling tools offered him free accounts, but that would add "scheduled by" attribution under his tweets, which he didn't want. He likes that it is simple: a schedule of slots you fill ahead of time, plus best-time calculation. He also likes evergreen re-posting of popular tweets.

chunks.heading: Twitter algorithm: use the exact topic keyword
chunks.text:
- He says the Twitter algorithm doesn't understand synonyms, only topic names. To trend in marketing you must literally use the word "marketing"; if you discuss it without the word, it doesn't work.
- Where to find topics: the "trending in..." topics in the home feed, or Twitter settings under content preferences, which lists every topic and subtopic (for example business, with startups, funding, entrepreneur, small business beneath).
- Use at least one topic keyword in every tweet you want to reach beyond your followers.
- Two ways past your circle: retweets (rare and a big investment) or a keyword plus a fast initial burst of likes. He recalls roughly 5 likes in about 10 minutes being enough, but isn't sure anymore.
- It worked at 300 followers. He says many people with great tweets get zero likes because they lack the early boost and the keyword.
- He now gets at least one tweet a week with more than 2,000 likes, and says that wouldn't happen without keywords.

chunks.heading: Paid channels failed; going all-in on Twitter
chunks.text:
- Google Ads: he spent $600 and made $0.
- Facebook ads: skipped, believing a meaningful test needs at least a couple of thousand dollars.
- Newsletter sponsorships: about $200 across roughly four indie-hacker newsletters, hard to track, no visible effect.
- His takeaway: as a builder who disliked marketing, he assumed he could just put money into ads. He says you can't pay money and make money without a lot of budget for testing; you have to hustle.
- Affiliates: he tried and failed before Twitter.
- He then spent about 8 hours a day on Twitter for six months, with no product changes for 10 months. He has since found processes that need less time and is building features again.

chunks.heading: What Twitter brings besides sales
chunks.text:
- SEO backlinks: he gets about one new backlink per day with no dedicated effort, from stories, memes, interviews and "accounts to follow" lists. His wife is starting SEO content this year, and he did the keyword research. He expects the two together to compound.
- Partnerships: Chad (CSAcorn), founder of Better Legal, which helps people form US LLCs, DMed him after Dagobert shared a struggle. Every Better Legal signup now gets an email recommending Logology for logos, and Dagobert pays him a commission.
- Opportunities like podcast interviews, and credibility.
- Community and mindset: finding hundreds of close peers and thousands of like-minded founders made him feel less alone and less negative, and showed him every founder makes mistakes.
- Logology costs $100, versus about $2,000 for a custom logo.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert shares how Logology, a logo and brand design service he runs with his wife, flopped at launch after building for nearly two years. He then found traction by spamming his link, going all-in on Twitter, and sharing his journey publicly, reaching roughly $2-3k/month. He also reflects on chasing money versus fulfillment.

chunks.heading: Money chasing, burnout, and the move to a startup
chunks.text:
- Dagobert started making money online in high school with fan sites. One for a French Idol contestant ranked first on the contestant's name in the domain. He placed a Google ad directly against the download link and made about $150 in one night around the final.
- He then freelanced as a web developer and, at 27, moved to San Francisco to get a US engineering job. He landed a dream job at $100k a year.
- After a few months of buying whatever he wanted, he got bored. His realization: "all this time all I wanted was to create stuff and be on an adventure," and with nothing left to chase, he lost that.
- He now says he doesn't want money for its own sake: "it's empty." He chased it for almost 15 years.
- At 29 he left the safe job to build a startup with his savings, having tried freelancing and employment. His view: staying in a safe job leads to being miserable, so the risk is worth taking to find some happiness.
- He describes being "both fulfilled and full of anxiety" while living off savings. In February 2022, selling about one logo per week, he considered going back to a job, then rejected it ("remember what it's like having a boss") and went all in again.

chunks.heading: Finding the idea and building the first product (2018 to 2020)
chunks.text:
- In September 2018 he saw a founder on Indie Hackers say he was "making a killing" with Logo Joy, an automated logo generator. His wife is a logo designer and he is an engineer, so they decided to build Logology together.
- Their plan was to start from scratch rather than copy Logo Joy. They had worked together before: she designed websites and he coded them.
- Progress was slow. His mother died in November 2018, which cost him about three months of productivity. He also "indulged" in engineering and building the perfect product.
- They launched in April 2020, about a year and a half after starting. He barely slept and kept perfecting the site overnight.

chunks.heading: Why the launch failed
chunks.text:
- They announced to a waiting list of 100 people, expecting roughly 50 sales. They got one sale, from a friend, then no traffic and no sales.
- His diagnosis: they were "psyched up about our own product thinking it's so amazing" and had no marketing plan beyond announcing it on Reddit and Indie Hackers.
- A third co-founder joined for about a year to do marketing. He posted on Reddit and Indie Hackers, and a few hit posts brought some sales. Then it died out, and people started complaining about repeat posting ("you just posted that last week").
- Once launch channels were exhausted, they did what he says every founder does without a marketing plan: built more features to fix it.
- Costs: they were about $50k down in savings. His father told him to stop and get a job. About 50 people had bought a logo after a year and many loved it, and he did not want a job again, so they kept going.

chunks.heading: Marketing he tried that failed
chunks.text:
- He avoided marketing because it's hard and he did not want to "write a sales letter" and convince people. He wanted the product to speak for itself.
- Google Ads produced zero sales. Sponsoring a few newsletters produced zero results.
- Realization in 2021: the missing piece was marketing. He still hated it and did not want another co-founder.

chunks.heading: What worked: spamming, then Twitter in public (May 2021)
chunks.text:
- His first approach was brute force: put the link everywhere. On Twitter he searched for posts like "what are you working on today?" and replied with Logology about 20 times a day. He did the same on Product Hunt discussion boards, Indie Hackers and Reddit. For a couple of weeks nothing happened.
- First break: someone on Twitter asked which CSS technology he used for his website. As a front-end engineer he answered and shared his link. It went viral, with about 1,000 visits in 24 hours and 2 sales in a day.
- Second break: a visitor on the website live chat said the logos were too expensive and that he could just screenshot the free branding course his wife spent a month writing. Dagobert, who had about 200 followers then, posted the screenshot on Twitter and it went viral. He also got a sale, possibly out of pity.
- Lesson: sharing what he was going through, the real struggle, worked on Twitter. He went all in, spending about 10 hours a day on it.

chunks.heading: Results and diversifying beyond Twitter
chunks.text:
- Revenue went from almost nothing to nearly $3k in his best month. It now hovers between $2k and $3k a month.
- He did not get more out of Twitter after the initial jump.
- Downside of Twitter: sales depend on posting. "If you don't tweet for one day, nobody comes to your website," which he finds exhausting.
- He is starting SEO. Twitter feeds it indirectly: podcast interviews (like this one) and articles written by people who found him on Twitter bring links to his site.
- Goal: spread sales across more sources so he can relax with "a good system."

chunks.heading: Recommendations
chunks.text: - Book: *Zero to One* by Peter Thiel, which he says he always comes back to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dago launches the new This Indie Life format with Nico, focused on the unglamorous side of bootstrapping. He shares lessons from his failed logo startup, why passive income is a myth, why indies should plan an exit, and how overwork and success highs derail founders.

chunks.heading: Dagobert's journey: from burnout to divorce to rebuilding
chunks.text:
Dagobert opens the episode by explaining the pivot of This Indie Life toward "the dark side of entrepreneurship". His most successful episode in year one was the one where he described burning out with his startup, which then led to his divorce.

- He says constant success content ("I just made $10,000 this month") makes him "start to feel like a failure real fast".
- His goal is a podcast where founders are honest that "nobody's above everyone else": everyone is struggling, in doubt, and having ups and downs.
