- He had been with the same partner 12 years (from 21 to 34) and is now divorcing her. He describes the aftermath as "brutal", lonely and scary, with rejection "in your face all the time", but also as a period of fast personal growth.

chunks.heading: Why his past logo startup lost to an AI-generated competitor
chunks.text:
Dagobert's previous startup sold logos. He contrasts it with a competitor that used AI image generators, produced dozens of logos instantly, charged a low price and promised no particular result.

- The competitor made about $85K in 3 months (roughly $20K from the app plus a ~$65K exit), more than Dagobert's startup made in 5 years.
- His own mistake: "we went after a market that doesn't have much money" and used the highest quality, with every logo designed by hand.
- Few buyers in that market appreciated the quality, so it was "kind of useless".
- He says the competitor spent about 20 times less and made about the same money. The lesson he draws is that people wanted the cheap, instant result at that price point in that market.

chunks.heading: Emotional attachment, family-restaurant thinking, and planning an exit
chunks.text:
Dagobert describes how he built his company with his wife and treated it as "our baby".

- They thought of it as "a family restaurant" and said they would never sell.
- That attachment led them to try to save something that was sinking. He calls it "too much emotion and attachment".
- His current view: if you want to stay indie, you need to plan an exit. If a product takes off (he uses $100K/month as an example), it attracts competitors and big players, and a solo founder who wants to avoid hiring ten people cannot fight them. "You either die or you exit."
- He sees exceptions like Peter Levels as very uncommon.
- Commoditization risk varies by product. Community and reputation products are harder to copy. He notes that a Twitter course built on being the reference in the indie maker world can't be copied.
- He cites Kevin O'Leary's idea that entrepreneurs who do it for money give up quickly, while those who do it for freedom keep fighting. He frames what founders want as freedom, not money.
- He also points out that a developer could reach roughly $200K+ at big US companies within about 5 years if money were the only goal.

chunks.heading: Working too hard: 70-hour weeks and the wrong product
chunks.text:
Dagobert explains why he stopped lifting and training after his first two years as a founder. Early on he did 5x5 StrongLifts at home with weights and plates, but food, sleep and training time all add up.

- His realization after about a year and a half: he needed to give "150% to even stay in the chance", so he trained less and then stopped for about two years.
- His peak was roughly 72 hours of work in a week, which was when he was close to burnout.
- His key lesson: "if you need to work this hard for this long, maybe it's the wrong product."
- For sustainable indie income (he uses $5K/month as an example), he argues you don't need to overwork. Once you have years of experience and skills, you can find a different product or revenue source without destroying your health. When you're 18 you should work your ass off to get skills.
- He believes that with his current experience he could get a few sales quickly on a new SaaS, whereas beginners face the same large quantity of things to learn (copywriting, marketing, shipping) no matter what.

chunks.heading: Indie as "hard mode": no assists, no cushion
chunks.text:
Dagobert compares indie life to the Doom nightmare difficulty.

- On hard difficulty you cannot stop moving, your brain has to change, and the game takes about 100 hours instead of 20.
- As an indie "we remove every assist, every helper". If you don't see sales on the Stripe dashboard, "then you suck. That's just how it is."
- This is why it feels like a roller coaster: when things go well it's all on you, so the highs and lows are extreme and hard to manage. One day you feel on top of the world and the next day, with no sales and no explanation, you feel like you suck.

chunks.heading: Handling the highs and lows: illusions, cockiness and stoicism
chunks.text:
Dagobert says the same pattern shows up in both sales and dating. You imagine the win will take you to "this ultimate place of freedom and happiness", then realize hours later that life is the same.

- Danger of the high: you get cocky and "stop doing the things that brought you here in the first place". He says this applies whether the high comes from a woman or from your company.
- His antidote is to accept the pain without collapsing and to not become cocky when you succeed. He calls it "kind of like stoicism".
- On bad days he says it happens to everyone, "even to the best". Not feeling like crap sometimes may mean you aren't challenging yourself.
- He uses the line "some days it rains, some days it's sunny".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dago explains why he and his wife closed their bootstrapped logo startup Logology after five years: no recurring revenue, constant customer-acquisition pressure, AI uncertainty and a health-wrecking burnout. His main lesson is to start from business fundamentals (demand, willingness to pay, acquisition cost) rather than a cool idea and hard work.

chunks.heading: Why Dagobert shut down Logology after five years
chunks.text:
- **Outcome:** Dagobert and his wife Lucy closed the logo design startup Logology after five years and almost all their savings. It had reached 3K per month in revenue, plus 5K per month from his Twitter course "Dominate Twitter".
- **Real problem:** the cost of living and running a business in France made that revenue "barely enough to survive". Profitability reached a few months earlier had already slipped back below survival level.
- **Recurring pressure:** the logo product had no recurring revenue, so they needed to find 100+ new customers every month. They considered a recurring model plus SEO, but AI uncertainty (both for acquiring customers and for designing logos) made them doubt it would be enough.
- **Why not raise money:** hiring a couple of people was another option, but after five years of fighting they were exhausted, out of motivation and out of money.

chunks.heading: Burnout and what overwork cost
chunks.text:
- In February 2023 Dagobert suffered a massive burnout. His heart rate went wild every time he stood up, and he spent weeks in bed, thinking it was long covid.
- Years of screen time without rest damaged his eyes. He gets dazzled by bright light (screens, traffic lights, sunny days) and will need glasses permanently.
- He worked around 80 hours a week for five years, with no time for hobbies, fun or romance. Even on rare vacations he kept thinking about getting the next customer.
- He says they "sacrificed everything we cared about just to reach success at any cost", and the dream of living on their own terms got lost along the way.

chunks.heading: Lesson: a good business matters more than a good idea or hard work
chunks.text:
- He admits they were idealistic and believed "having a good idea and working hard was enough to succeed".
- His conclusion: "all that matters is: is it a good business?" That means:
  - Is there demand?
  - Are customers paying enough?
  - Can you acquire customers at a good enough cost?
- He calls this "the boring stuff" and says founders avoid it in favor of the fantasy of building a cool product (his example: "that would be so cool if there was a new AI copywriting tool").
- Only after finding a good niche or market should you ask whether your idea is good and how hard to work. Look at competition and risks first.
- Logology competed in a crowded logo niche and struggled to make ends meet from launch day. They also made bad strategic decisions that forced constant overwork.
- His summary: "we're constantly swimming against the fact that it's not a good business to be in." He insists he can't be blamed for lack of effort: "I really tried my best."
- Even a successful solo business can go down in three months, so starting from a weak business makes the vulnerability worse. He says a founder's work is "never over".

chunks.heading: Denial and the Twitter feedback loop
chunks.text:
- He says he and Lucy were in denial for at least two years. Some denial can help (he sees value in faking it till you make it for about six months), but theirs went on far too long.
- Twitter made it worse. Good feedback, interactions and networking made it feel like they were progressing, and his Twitter success let other people back up the belief that they were doing well.
- The burnout was the wake-up call that ended the denial.
- He now wants to tweet about mistakes instead of successes, because Startup Twitter is almost entirely success stories that friends leave because they stop being useful. He had about 30 drafts of mistake tweets ready.
- He also described stopping tweeting for weeks because he felt like "a loser and a failure", and his fear that people would lose interest if he stopped sharing motivating tweets.

chunks.heading: The next step: product manager at a small startup
chunks.text:
- Dagobert went back to a job, starting the following week on a trial period. He had avoided this for five years and said he never thought he'd do it.
- He used to be a developer but was bored by having little control, "just here to execute". Researching roles, he found product management, which he describes as the "CEO of the product":
  - speaking to customers
  - defining features and strategy
  - working with developers (easy because he is a dev) and designers (easy because he is a designer)
- He deliberately chose a small startup, where a product manager can oversee the whole product and focus on growing it, unlike big companies where PMs handle a single feature.
- Expected benefits: an end to the crazy hours and constant financial pressure, and work that can become enjoyable again. In France the standard week is around 35 hours, which he notes is less than what he worked on "vacation".
- He admits fears: losing the no-alarm-clock lifestyle and being stuck five days a week working for others. He says he knows to "curb my enthusiasm" because he has bootstrapped startups.

chunks.heading: Plans for the future
chunks.text:
- He expects to come back to startups someday but has no motivation now and needs time to recover and live a simpler life.
- Next time he wants to build with at least one co-founder who is "completely different" from him and Lucy. Logology felt solo even as a couple because they lacked business skills.
- He wants to stay in France and network locally for co-founders, noting he has many Twitter followers but almost no networking contacts in France.
- Lucy keeps running the site and may return to custom logo design.

chunks.heading: Takeaways on community and money shocks
chunks.text:
- When he hit rock bottom and stopped tweeting, follower count "wasn't worth much". The friends he made on Twitter, dozens of whom supported him over DMs, gave insights and perspective and "made it 10 times easier to find a way out".
- On financial volatility, he says that as an indie founder an unexpected cost hits you directly (e.g. losing 5K to broken equipment), unlike an employee whose boss pays. His view: "it's never over, you always have to hustle... you can rest for like three months tops."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dago relaunches This Indie Life solo after burning out, divorcing and leaving a job. He picks content (podcast, book, course, newsletter) as the fastest route to 4K a month, explains why going solo lowered his required revenue, and why he now shares the hard parts and takes sponsors.

chunks.heading: Why Dagobert is going all-in on content, not another startup
chunks.text:
Dagobert quit his job and now has about 8 months of French unemployment benefits to build a sustainable solo income. His only revenue is a Twitter course that brings about $500 a month. He needs $4K a month to live.

- He rejects starting another startup: "I'm tired of it already." He spent 5 years on his own startup with his ex-wife, then 8 months at another startup, both stuck in the uphill grind of finding product-market fit and chasing customers.
- His stated focus for the next months is survival, not scale: get back to indie hacking full-time and avoid going back to a job.
- He picks content because it is the quickest path to money and is "only one thing": writing, thinking and connecting with people. It avoids the code, product and marketing split of a startup.

chunks.heading: The 4-part income plan to reach $4K a month
chunks.text:
Dagobert lists the levers he is pulling at once:

- **Podcast:** one episode a week, with sponsors.
- **Book:** finish the book he started on all the mistakes he made with his first startup, then start selling it.
- **Twitter course:** update it into something like "how to dominate X", which he admits "sounds pretty porny" but thinks is a good title.
- **Newsletter:** a weekly deep thought about entrepreneurship, his best meme of the week, and a short journey update. Linked from his Twitter bio.
- He also diversifies onto other social platforms.

chunks.heading: Why he drops the paycheck-style startup math: $4K vs $10K
chunks.text:
Dagobert explains why his burnout risk is lower now.

- With his ex-partner, the two of them had to run a formal company. In France that meant heavier taxes, so they needed about $10K a month in revenue to make a basic living.
- Alone, he can use the auto-entrepreneur (freelancer) status, which has lower taxes on revenue. He lives well on $4K a month, the same standard as $10K a month before.
- He was the one responsible for bringing in revenue and customers, restarting from zero every month, on top of social media and product work.
- A second cause of burnout was being pulled in two opposite directions: viral social media and community engagement on one side, deep focused product building on the other. He says context switching between them was impossible for him.
- Now he focuses on one kind of work, so he is still wary of burning out again but sees the main causes as removed.

chunks.heading: Why he now takes sponsors
chunks.text:
- Earlier he refused sponsors because it "felt dirty". The podcast was meant as free promotion for his startup Logology, and he wanted to look like a "pure founder" so people would buy his products.
- After his burnout he calls that "the stupidest thing". He treats the podcast as a business and needs to make money.
- Rules for sponsors: only apps and products he loves and thinks his audience could love, with the same transparent, authentic tone: "I got to make money."
- Audience size he cites: about 750 listeners per episode, counting the full episode posted on Twitter, YouTube and the audio platforms.

chunks.heading: Content strategy: honest struggle instead of success stories
chunks.text:
Dagobert's differentiator is sharing the dark side of indie work.

- He argues social media is full of success stories, and that seeing only the positives makes him "feel like [ __ ]". He wants a community of founders rather than people sharing wins for likes.
- Each weekly episode is either an interview with an indie maker about the difficult parts of entrepreneurship, or a solo deep reflection on the same theme. He doesn't enjoy guest-only podcasts where the host never shares his own story.
- Recurring topics: stress, anxiety, fear, and the impact on personal life (divorce, relationships, health, lost sleep, quitting workouts).
- Examples from founders he has spoken to: one has an app with thousands of paying users but risks burnout from hiring and spending time on accounting; another loses sleep when he goes 2-3 days without new sales.
- He has five big indie makers lined up as guests.
- Audience interaction: an "Indie Hotline" page on his site where listeners send audio, video or text (10 MB upload limit on the free form tool, with an optional anonymous checkbox). He plays and reacts to the messages in solo episodes. He plans to upgrade the form once he makes more than $500 a month.

chunks.heading: What he learned from the burnout recovery year
chunks.text:
- After his February 2023 burnout he returned to a job in June 2023 as a product manager at a Paris startup, working fully remote. It was a deliberate recovery job and let him build unemployment entitlement (about one month of benefit per month worked, 6 months minimum to unlock).
- He rebuilt health, social circle and finances during this period, including joining a local co-working space with entrepreneurs and creators. He says real-life friends help his health more than online ones.
- His boss reacted to his resignation notice by saying he could leave in two weeks, rather than staying 3-6 months as he had offered. Dagobert says it hurt his ego and wrecked his plan for more months of salary, but he saw it as a "cold shower" he was ready for.
- He says he got addicted to the "reality" of being indie, being exposed with a tiger looming, and calls it the only real life.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dago hosts a candid talk with Lukas (Stage Timer) about burnout, therapy and comparison on Twitter. His own takeaways: perfectionism and pride sank his last startup, therapy exposes ego-driven product mistakes, and social growth depends on where your audience actually is. Mostly mindset, with a few distribution points.

chunks.heading: Dagobert's burnout: how it happened and what he changed
chunks.text:
- Dagobert's burnout was driven by perfectionism, ego, and a fear of failing, more than by the work itself.
- He spent 6 months building useless features because he wanted the product to be perfect and was scared of failing. He says a therapist could have saved him those six months.
- His last startup failed partly because he tried to do everything perfectly and spent months on things that could have taken weeks or days.
- He admits he wanted to be CEO and kept control of everything, telling himself it made life easier for his then co-founder and wife. In reality he was "so scared of losing control", and everything sat on his shoulders.
- When he burned out and collapsed, everything collapsed with him, because he had put all the responsibility on himself. This was a big part of the end of the relationship and the startup.
- His body kept the damage. He says he spends hours a day consciously blinking so his eyes don't hurt, from years of staring at screens too long, too focused.
- He used to think burnout was all mindset and that he could push through. He now says you can push until something physically breaks.

chunks.heading: Therapy as a founder tool
chunks.text:
- Dagobert has been in therapy for about six months. He says everyone told him to go and he first thought he didn't need it, because he already journaled and meditated.
- His point: knowing something is wrong is different from having a trusted professional tell you "this is the mistake you're making". It "changes everything".
- He compares it to the gym: "it's like mental health", so there's no reason not to do it.
- His therapist is Argentinian and based in northern France. A session lasts 1.5 hours:
  - About 40 minutes of normal talk therapy.
  - Then she asks where he feels the issue in his body (usually chest or neck) and works on it for 30-40 minutes with a kind of massage meant to heal and release what's blocked.
  - Then a 10-minute debrief.
  - It is so intense he can only go about twice a month.
- He says the body work is the "magic part": for two weeks afterwards his posture and body change without effort.
- A therapist helps founders because most mistakes are not knowledge problems. "We know what we need to do but we don't really want to do it", because of ego or pride. Someone outside the indie-hacker bubble can show you that.
- On the second session, his therapist showed him what he had said and pointed toward leaving his wife. He says the answer was "right there" and felt too scary to say out loud.
- Social media is an echo chamber where everyone repeats the same things to support each other. A therapist outside it makes things feel less big.

chunks.heading: Rules for his current work rhythm
chunks.text:
- Dagobert goes to a co-working space and gets a rhythm and friends from it. He takes the long French lunch break with them, even when he feels like he should keep working.
- He walks 20 minutes each way, puts on AirPods and sings in the street.
- That walk helped him drop a stressful problem: Twitter wouldn't let him upload an episode before a recording. He decided "I'll figure it out tomorrow" and arrived calm and present instead of rushing and multitasking.
- Lesson: "we need more quiet and more calm in our lives." Stress leads to wrong priorities, rushed work and mistakes.
- If he started another startup with a co-founder, he would do couples-style therapy with them at least monthly. He sees co-founders as a relationship like a marriage.

chunks.heading: Saying no instead of yes to everything
chunks.text:
- Dagobert says that at his peak he replied to every Twitter reply and DM and said no to nobody, because he feared missing out.
- Now he ignores free offers (free videos, free content, cold emails). His reason: "it's not free. I have to spend time getting into it", and it diverts focus from his own agenda.
- He found he lost much less engagement than he feared. He credits a strong community who care about him.
- He thinks the fear came from childhood-style fear of being abandoned: if you stop being active, people forget you.

chunks.heading: Money versus following his heart
chunks.text:
- Dagobert had just left his job with only a little money saved. He had also just separated from his wife, so he had little support system.
- He was offered paid work. Daniel Vassallo offered him $4K per month to be an ambassador for Small Bets. Others offered a lot of money for a few memes.
- He says saying yes to money feels like the safe way, since "I can't fail". But if it's not what your heart wants, you "end up not in the right life", then burn out and become unhappy.
- Since the burnout he is "not willing to compromise" on that anymore. He is trying to balance where his heart wants to go with financial stability.

chunks.heading: Fixing perfectionism in his podcast and getting joy back
chunks.text:
- Dagobert paused This Indie Life for a month after the Nico interview. The reason: editing the Moo episode took 3 days, and the pain of that made him procrastinate. He had recorded 5 more interviews meanwhile.
- After posting about it on Twitter, people told him he didn't need a perfect edit. He now does a clean edit and publishes, which takes about 4 hours instead of 3 days, so he can do one episode per week.
- His view: the value of the podcast is the content and the original, unfiltered conversations with founders, not production polish.
- He tells his sponsor he'd rather not take the money some weeks: "this week I'm not feeling it", because he wants to keep the joy.
- He wants to code again just for fun, with no goal of making money. He had started coding at about 15, and it was fun until it became a freelance job. He is a Ruby on Rails fan.
- His idea: build something useless, like a movie-ranking app, only for himself. He notes the trap of turning every hobby into a boilerplate, template or product.
- Rule of thumb: when a hobby becomes a way to make money, it gets hard to have a hobby again.

chunks.heading: Distribution and platform choice
chunks.text:
- Dagobert's lesson from burning out on Twitter: he went all in on one platform and depended on it for traffic and sales. When Elon took over, things changed and it was very stressful.
- This time he diversifies, but he says what matters is not the type of content but who uses the platform: "who's listening and where are they hanging out."
- His audience is founders, small entrepreneurs, startup founders and indie hackers. They are not really on Instagram or TikTok.
- His best Twitter memes got hundreds of thousands of views but only about two likes on Instagram.
- Threads surprised him: with only about 100 followers there, one meme got about 60 likes, and he enjoys it.
- He has about 85K followers on Twitter.
- Tip: if you fail on one platform, maybe your people are simply not there. Go where your audience is.

chunks.heading: Authenticity on Twitter
chunks.text:
- Dagobert says posts where he shares his struggles do very well because they are engaging and real.
- He warns that authenticity can become clickbait too: "I'm starting to figure out how to make people cry."
- He wants to stay mindful of that trap, and thinks the newer algorithm rewards human, emotional or funny content over only showing off revenue.
- On comparison: he says that opening Twitter and seeing other founders succeed while you fail makes you feel bad, and that LinkedIn and TikTok are even worse.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dago explains why he burned out after launching his course, how he batches two months of tweets in one week, and why links kill tweet reach unless you make people curious or incentivize engagement. He also shares how 10K followers changed perceived credibility, and why living and building real stories beats rehashing strategy.

chunks.heading: Burnout comes from too many open threads, not too much work
chunks.text:
- After pushing hard on his Twitter course (Dominate Twitter), Dagobert hit a down period over Christmas.
- He says the cause was mostly lack of clarity: "when I get too many things I get lost and I lose direction and when I lose direction I lose productivity and I burn out quickly."
- The pile-up included course improvements, a Logology version 2, tweet writing, and company admin and accounting he had ignored for months.
- His fix:
  - Clear the neglected admin.
  - Decide the course is "good enough" and stop improving it, with only small updates a few times a year.
  - Write two months of content ahead so he can move on to something else.
- Once the backlog was done he felt relaxed and free to start something new.

chunks.heading: Batching: a week of writing for two months of tweets
chunks.text:
- Dagobert's usual system is one concentrated week of writing roughly two months of tweets and memes ahead of time.
- He had skipped it for a stretch, and the tweets posted in that gap were low quality. They got far fewer likes even though impressions held up.
- He would rather stop posting than "post low quality just to post."
- For the next batch he plans to:
  - Add long-form threads.
  - Add a few meme threads.
  - Write shorter, more authoritative advice-style tweets, "better" versions of the platitude format.

chunks.heading: Threads: value, not a growth hack
chunks.text:
- Dagobert was long wary of threads because they feel like a growth tactic, and most of them are "boring as [ __ ]."
- He has written only two in his whole time on Twitter, and people loved both. He says that is because threads are a different way of bringing value, not because they are a hack.
- Planned thread: his full strategy for launching the course, start to finish, since many people asked how it succeeded.
- He also plans more meme threads, because one went very popular a few months earlier.

chunks.heading: Follower count changes how people read you
chunks.text:
- Reaching 10K followers was, for Dagobert, the biggest shift in how people perceive him.
- Sales of his product rose "overnight" because 10K made him look more credible.
- At a larger size, his old long personal "story tweets" stopped landing. Followers now expect advice from him, not just stories.
- He says a tweet from someone with 100 followers carries a different weight than the same tweet from someone with 50K.

chunks.heading: Why polished content goes stale: build, fail, then tweet
chunks.text:
- Early on, Dagobert was deep in building Logology, so his tweets were raw, lived and resonated.
- Over time he refined tweeting into a craft, so it became less spontaneous. He thinks readers can feel that it is "rehashed stuff that I already said last year."
- Diagnosis: he spent a year mostly tweeting and had nothing new to say. "You can't [ __ ] people," he adds, and he isn't trying to.
- His remedy is to stop spending all his time tweeting and go build Logology v2: get "slapped again by reality," experience failures, and tweet about those stories.
- Rule he draws: spend time building or experiencing things, then tweet about them.

chunks.heading: Links in tweets: get engagement with or without the link
chunks.text:
- Mechanism: a link doesn't hide the tweet. People click it, leave, and don't engage with the tweet, so it gets no extra visibility and dies.
- He gives three ways around it:
  1. Make the tweet itself interesting and curiosity-provoking, then put the link in a follow-up tweet. People engage first, then go looking.
  2. Add an incentive to engage even after clicking. For his course's Black Friday sale, the offer was 40% off, with 60% off if you retweeted.
  3. His usual approach: keep the link in his bio and make people curious enough to click his profile. For example, "here's a new episode of my podcast doing this and that." People who want to support him will engage and visit his profile.

chunks.heading: Video clips with subtitles
chunks.text:
- Dagobert recalls a podcast he guested on two years earlier. The host posted very short (about 15-second) clips with highly visible subtitles.
- A clip of him explaining the Twitter algorithm got about 150 likes and brought the host many listeners.
- His takeaway: a short, valuable bite with subtitles can do well and make people want to tune in to the full show. Without subtitles, it won't work as well.

chunks.heading: Validating a product by selling it publicly
chunks.text:
- Dagobert's takeaway from watching a product tested on Twitter: share the product with an audience and see instantly whether people want it.
- If they don't, you avoid wasting time. If they pay, "they validate it with their money" and it is clearly going to be a successful product.
- He adds that showing a real product being built is more exciting to an audience of indie makers and startup founders than content about services, because they all want to create things.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert reflects on three months at a job, why it never fully satisfies him, and how comparing himself to lifestyle-focused indie hackers fed his burnout. He decides to build things that help indies and freelancers, reviews why Logology failed, and weighs pivots and a course update.

chunks.heading: The job honeymoon ends after three months and the trade-off becomes clear
chunks.text:
- Dagobert took a job at Abisol and says that after about three months the honeymoon is over. He likes the team, has autonomy, feels he brings value, and is glad to be paid.
- He still frames it plainly: it is a job, and he doesn't want to spend 40 hours a week of his life on one.
- He has made peace with it. He sees the job as stability and income, not as something that has to fulfil him.
- Early on he put all his eggs in the job. After about two months he took a week off and felt deeply low, "what's the point of living" low, which he traces to expecting the job to fulfil him.
- Once he lowered his expectations, he got more productive at work. His approach became to complete the mission, help others and do the job well, without hoping it would give him deeper meaning.

chunks.heading: Why building his own things feels different from job work
chunks.text:
- Dagobert wants to build things that come from inside him. He describes it as less like being an artist and more like giving something of himself.
- Example: he rebuilt Abisol's homepage, which is now in an A/B test against the old version. He spent weeks and months understanding the product and the value to convert visitors.
- Yet it isn't the same as the homepage for his own course, which carries his style, his voice, and a design that is on brand with his personality.
- On his own work he feels people see him. On the job he is spreading the company's message.
- His earlier freelancing, before Logology, felt like constantly running after money. He rarely had a stretch where he could switch work off and on.

chunks.heading: Burnout came from imitating the lifestyle indie hackers
chunks.text:
- He identifies a cause of his burnout: comparing himself to and imitating Pieter Levels, Daniel Vassallo, Jon Yongfook and Danny Postma. They make a lot of money and promote the lifestyle side of indie hacking.
- Daniel Vassallo often talks about working only a couple of hours a day. Dagobert says if he did that he would not be happy.
- His real driver is to contribute, help and support others, and that is how he connects with the world and feels happy. He did this for a long time on Twitter by supporting and connecting with people.
- He doesn't want to build a product only because it is trendy. He wants to create things that help people, specifically indies, freelancers and solopreneurs.
- This clarity helps him accept the job: it gives him financial stability, so he doesn't need a side project to make money.

chunks.heading: What he learned from Logology
chunks.text:
- Logology sold almost 900 logos, and he is proud of that.
- He thinks it failed partly because the team focused mostly on how to help people without money get a good logo, instead of on how to build a good business.
- He says he has a hard time losing and still believes Logology can succeed.

chunks.heading: Side project ideas he is exploring
chunks.text:
- **Logology pivot:** a design AI assistant with a ChatGPT-style chat interface, built on Logology's accumulated design knowledge. A user says they are building a product but are bad at design. The tool asks a few questions about the product and guides them toward a better look.
- **Marketing version:** the same assistant idea applied to marketing, which he says is more his thing, to help people market their product.
- **Course update:** his Twitter course has basically stopped selling. Now that Twitter is called X, it is obvious the course hasn't been updated in a year, which he thinks scares buyers. He wants to ship a free "version 2" update of roughly 1 to 1.5 hours on adapting to the new algorithm.
- None of this is committed yet. He says he has "nothing clear for now" and will work on it in evenings and weekends.

chunks.heading: Stability, savings and the risk of overcommitting
chunks.text:
- Going full-time on Logology worked because he had savings and knew he had to make it work. He calls that both very helpful and incredibly stressful.
- He sees no clean solution: side projects are hard to stay motivated on week after week, while full-time indie work is stressful on money.
- He says he tends to get excited about something, pour everything into it, get things done for a while, then retreat. A steady paycheck gives him stability against that pattern.
- He acknowledges he needs the job's income and can't simply stop the job to chase side projects. He plans to see how he manages a 40-hour job alongside side projects.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: After losing $100k and his marriage to a failed startup, Dagobert Renouf resets his approach. He rebuilds health and runway, then monetizes existing assets (audience, podcast, course, consulting) to reach about $6k/month before risking another startup.

chunks.heading: Rebuilding after a $100k failure: financial freedom before the next startup
chunks.text: Dagobert's previous bootstrapped startup failed. He lost his life savings ($100k+), his marriage ended in divorce, and he burned out badly enough to need months of rest, meditation and therapy. He took an 8-month job, moved, and made real-life friends to get stability back. He describes his health as back at about 80% and says he is ready to build again, but he is also scared.

chunks.heading: How Dagobert sees the risk of startups
chunks.text:
- He says running a startup is "10x harder" than the media success stories suggest.
- Success is never fully in the founder's control, even with validated ideas and a polished product.
- Building a startup is a bet: you win rarely and lose often, and the game continues until you sell or quit.
- Even with product-market fit and revenue growth, things can collapse at any time:
  - Social or SEO algorithm changes can cut traffic by 90% and kill growth.
  - Platforms you depend on (payments, APIs) can change pricing or ban you for no valid reason.
  - OpenAI can launch a feature that makes your product obsolete.
- His metaphor: a founder is "the captain of a ship in a never-ending storm" who must constantly avoid the rocks.
- His reason for entrepreneurship was "more freedom and joy out of life, not less", so he won't repeat the same ordeal.

chunks.heading: Safety net before taking risk
chunks.text:
- He is leaving his job and will receive French unemployment benefits, which cover living expenses for 7 months.
- He also keeps a $20k emergency fund in case anything goes wrong.
- He will not put all his hopes for financial freedom into one "crazy startup idea" again. Instead he wants "the most efficient way to get revenue without selling my time."

chunks.heading: Monetizing assets he already built
chunks.text:
From his last startup he kept three assets:

- A social following of 85K people.
- A podcast with about 750 listeners per episode.
- A Twitter course that still sells $500/month.

He admits that because he was obsessed with growing the startup rather than with financial freedom, he missed obvious revenue opportunities from these assets. Now he sees them clearly.

chunks.heading: The four small bets
chunks.text:
1. Write a short ebook on his failures and lessons learned, and sell it to founders who follow him.
2. Accept paid sponsors on the podcast.
3. Update the Twitter course to bring it back to $2-3k per month, the level before the X rebrand.
4. Offer $1000/hour consulting calls on social media strategy.

He thinks these four bets can reach about $6k per month, mostly on autopilot. That is enough to cover taxes, living expenses and emergencies and give him time and financial freedom.

chunks.heading: Content creation as the stepping stone
chunks.text:
- He admits being a content creator "isn't as sexy as a startup founder", but sees it as the right next step.
- The logic: get stable, sustainable income first, then be "in a better position to take the risk of building startups again."
- He plans to document the journey in a weekly newsletter with a deep lesson about entrepreneurship, his best meme of the week, and journey updates.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf shares how he and his wife built Logology, an automated logo and brand identity tool, after two years building and two years struggling with marketing. Twitter, used to share his founder journey, became the channel that finally worked. He also covers timeboxing, slow growth and building in public.

chunks.heading: Starting Logology from a shared design and dev partnership
chunks.text:
Dagobert Renouf started Logology with his wife in 2018 as a passion project. They wanted a business that used both their talents so they would be happy to come to work every day. As a team of one designer and one developer, they settled on an online tool in the design space.

- His wife was a freelance designer specializing in logo and brand identity design. She worked with startups and noticed early-stage companies often couldn't afford her services.
- They looked for a way to make it cheaper without losing quality. They landed on automating the brand research and design work, which cut the price by 10x.
- His rule of thumb: the best ideas come from problems you've noticed first-hand.
- They spent 2 years building the product and 2 more years learning how to market it.
- Logology is now an established online tool in the indie startup community. It helps dozens of founders every month figure out their brand identity and logo design.

chunks.heading: Twitter as the marketing channel that finally worked
chunks.text:
Dagobert spent the first 2.5 years struggling to find customers. Paid ads and sponsorships produced no growth. In summer 2021 he started tweeting about his startup journey.

- He went from 150 to 40k+ followers in a bit over a year, simply by talking about the lessons he learns on the startup journey.
- He noticed more people visiting his website, talking about the product and recommending it to other founders.
- He made it part of his daily routine and now spends about 2 hours a day on it.
- Results he credits to it: 10x more traffic per day, invitations to 10+ podcasts, and new partners.
- He calls Twitter "an under-rated marketing strategy for new founders" and "the game changer."

chunks.heading: Share your journey publicly to open doors
chunks.text:
Dagobert recommends every founder start talking about and sharing their journey with the public.

- It feels weird at first but builds up over time and opens new doors: finding customers, getting new partnerships, even investors.
- His framing: "You are the public face of your company and have a lot to win by connecting with the world directly."
- He sees this as the thing he does over and over and recommends everyone else do.

chunks.heading: Surviving a marketing failure by trying new ideas
chunks.text:
His main failure was marketing. He couldn't figure it out and felt like a huge failure because of it.

- He almost quit after 2 years, believing he wasn't the right person for the job.
- He didn't want to quit, so he kept trying different marketing ideas.
- One day he found the right one: growing a Twitter audience.
- His lesson: even if you fail at something for a long time, keep trying and you could finally succeed.

chunks.heading: Slow, small growth beats rocketship pressure
chunks.text:
Dagobert's contrarian belief is "You don't need to go fast to succeed. All you need is to never quit."

- Every year he wastes months not working on the right things, or stressing and procrastinating about the future, yet Logology grows every year.
- He argues it's time to loosen up on the need to grow like a unicorn or rocketship.
- Building a small business that moves slowly and allows mistakes gives him more happiness.
- He hopes to see more people quit traditional careers and build their own thing, dreaming of a future where 30% of the population works for themselves.
- He wishes he had started sooner. At 20 he wanted to build things but chickened out; he took the plunge at 28 and found it "was all I ever wanted and not as scary as I thought."

chunks.heading: Daily routine, timeboxing and time tracking
chunks.text:
Dagobert splits his day into two parts.

- First part: communicating and promoting the product to other startup founders, mainly by building an audience on Twitter.
- Second part: either writing marketing content or building and improving the product.
- He has tracked his time precisely for 10 years and timeboxes everything. He started while freelancing, to know how much time to bill each client.
- Over the years he saw it helped his own productivity: timeboxing stops him getting sucked into a mindless task for hours.
- He uses llamalife.co, a simple productivity app focused on timeboxing, to plan and accomplish the right things each day.

chunks.heading: Generating ideas and working style
chunks.text:
Dagobert has his best ideas while meditating and relaxing, which is hard to balance with the need to be productive.

- His strategy is to alternate between periods of thinking up new ideas and periods of intense work to make them happen.
- His favorite quote, from a French painter: "I like the rule that corrects emotion." To him creativity is the source of effort but needs boundaries to come to life.
- He recommends Peter Thiel's *Zero to One*, noting he only read the first third because the rest didn't apply to him, which shows how much value is in the first chapters.
- His best recent $100 spend was LED lights to improve webcam and video quality: "the result is so much better now that I wonder why I waited for so long."
- An idea he'd give away: a social book notes app where readers take notes, share a page of books and notes, and earn affiliate revenue from recommended books.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert Renouf, a bootstrapped founder short on cash, asked his audience for help paying for his wedding and turned their joke into a stunt: selling logo spots on his suit to fellow entrepreneurs for about 10,000 euros. The stunt shows how to use a community, persistence and quality execution, and it led to an unexpected sales job.

chunks.heading: Putting logos on a wedding suit: turning a funding problem into community and a job
chunks.text:
Dagobert Renouf was a bootstrapping entrepreneur for seven years (no outside funding). Over the summer of 2025 he launched a solo startup that wasn't going well, and he was running out of money. He wanted to marry his Russian fiancée, who he met almost two years earlier, and visa issues pushed them to speed up the wedding. He couldn't afford a wedding but refused to give up on either the wedding or the startup.

He posted to his social media community about his entrepreneur journey: "I have to find a way to pay for my wedding. No idea how I'm going to do it." He said the minimum wedding he could do was 4,000 euros.

chunks.heading: How the idea came out of an audience post
chunks.text:
- A famous entrepreneur friend in his community offered to loan him the 4,000 euros, with no obligation to repay if he couldn't. Dagobert says the friend "just wanted to support" him.
- Someone joked that if he needed help, he should put their logo on his suit. Dagobert notes that in an entrepreneur community "everybody wants to promote themselves. That's what we do."
- He took the joke seriously. His reasoning: after years in business, "You've got to get out of your comfort zone. You try crazy shit if you want to make it."
- He posted the offer on X, and dozens of people said they wanted a logo on his suit.

chunks.heading: Selling and pricing the spots
chunks.text:
- He sold spots at about 300 euros on average.
- In total he sold about 10,000 euros' worth of logo placements.
- 26 entrepreneurs ended up supporting the suit, and he knew almost all of them personally.
- Selling was harder than he expected, in part because he had to convince people that his fiancée was on board.
- Many backers told him to keep the money and skip the logo. He insisted on doing the suit anyway. He describes it as a wedding gift between entrepreneurs.

chunks.heading: Making the idea acceptable to his fiancée
chunks.text:
- She hated it at first. All she saw was people on X joking about it and making fun.
- What changed her mind was reframing it: the logos were a way to bring his community to their wedding.
- Her condition: only companies he loved, mostly indie companies and people he knew.

chunks.heading: Executing it so it looks good
chunks.text:
- Once committed, Dagobert wanted it to look good, not like a joke. He hired a talented but expensive stylist friend, quoted at about 5,000 euros.
- The final logo list was set at the end of August, with the wedding in October.
- Printing logos directly on the suit would have required prototypes and more time, so they used embroidery instead.
- The result was a high-quality suit that "doesn't look like a joke" in person, and family and friends loved it.
- During the wedding he was more stressed than his wife because he felt he owed sponsors visible logos in the photos and videos.

chunks.heading: Persistence through public criticism
chunks.text:
- Dagobert says it took months of posting about the suit, and half the responses each time said things like "This is so bad. This is disgusting."
- He sometimes felt he was the only one who saw the beauty in it, because entrepreneurship is his life: "There's nothing on the suit I don't like. I can almost see the face of every founder associated with their company."
- His takeaway: "At first, they think you're crazy, and then it seems obvious." He says this was the first time he experienced that pattern as an entrepreneur.

chunks.heading: The unexpected result: a sales job
chunks.text:
- The cofounder of Comp AI, an acquaintance, kept replying to Dagobert's suit posts asking to put his company's logo on it.
- Dagobert had also realized he could do sales. The cofounder told him, "Let's get you a sales job."
- Dagobert now works in tech sales at the startup Comp AI, based in Lille, France.
- He says he couldn't see any way of living other than entrepreneurship for years, and that without the suit, "I would have never gotten this job."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dagobert recounts building 100K X followers while his 5-year startup never exceeded $4K/month. Audience helped early (to $3K MRR) but hit diminishing returns at 10K followers, and chasing followers made him neglect fixing the product and building other channels. Success requires a real problem, a great product, and at least one durable distribution channel.

chunks.heading: Why Dagobert says 100K followers didn't make his startup succeed
chunks.text:
- Dagobert has 100K followers on X, yet the startup he built for 5 years never made more than $4K/month.
- He went viral often and got 8-10K visitors per month, but the product "just wasn't solving a big enough problem."
- Six years after starting his startup journey, he was making barely $1K per month despite the audience.
- His initial product died, and his Twitter course gradually lost momentum despite updates and good reviews, as X kept getting worse.

chunks.heading: How his audience helped early, then hit diminishing returns
chunks.text:
- Building an audience helped grow revenue from $300 to $3,000 per month at the beginning, which he calls "a game changer" at the time.
- After reaching about 10K followers, he only got diminishing returns on the time he spent.
- Sales stopped growing, and he had to spend 2+ hours per day on Twitter just to maintain revenue.
- He says that at that point he should have stepped back, fixed the product, and built other distribution channels.

chunks.heading: The mistake: chasing followers instead of sales
chunks.text:
- Instead of chasing sales, he started chasing followers and tried to become an "influencer."
- This led to spending around 4 hours a day creating content and engaging, which was never his dream. It made him miserable and led to a massive burnout.
- It caused him to neglect the hard work of fixing his product and building other distribution channels.
- He doesn't regret everything: he became a good writer, made founder friends who support him, and got his first taste of success from a Twitter course built for his audience.

chunks.heading: Why followers are a consequence, not the cause, of success
chunks.text:
- He warns against assuming that a successful person with lots of followers owes their success to the followers (unless they only sell info products or boilerplates).
- His examples are @dannypostmaa and @tdinh_me, both with 100K+ followers. He says they succeed because:
  - their products solve real problems
  - they build long-term acquisition channels like affiliation or SEO
- Their followers are a consequence of sharing their journey toward success, not the reason for it.

chunks.heading: His formula for making it big
chunks.text:
- To make it big you need to solve a real problem, build a great product, and figure out at least one distribution channel. "There is no way around it."
- Going viral and getting followers won't be "the magic bullet" for a startup.

chunks.heading: How much audience-building he recommends
chunks.text:
- Hustling to a few thousand followers at the beginning is great, and he recommends every founder do it.
- Benefits he lists: making friends in the community, opening doors for partnerships and media coverage like podcasts, and getting initial traffic for everything you build.
- Once you are somewhat established, he says time is better spent "in the trenches" doing the hard work of growing a real business.
- He's now doing that again after years of getting carried away, enjoys starting from scratch, and says he has never felt better.

- changes in social or SEO algorithms can reduce traffic by 90% and kill growth
- platforms I depend on to build my app (payment, APIs) can change their pricing model or decide to ban me for no valid reason

Big fan of Rob (seriously, he's a genuine one). But just want to point out a reason it works well for him is because he's selling a tweet scheduler, on twitter!

That gives him a huge advantage: he just post about his product, and gets free visibility to a 100% qualified audience.

The more he posts, the more he grows, and the more his audience thinks his product is legit and buys it.

If he was doing the exact same thing, but selling a Typeform alternative? Growth would probably be 10x slower.

Because only 10% of people who saw his post would be in the market for it, vs 100% for a tweet scheduler.

So he'd have to find another distribution channel, which is where most entrepreneurs struggle.

Not saying this to disqualify him, I genuinely think he's awesome.

Just a heads up for the kids thinking being good at twitter is enough to grow your product.

99% of the time it's not.

Good luck everyone.
